plan.summary: Abbott's CRM division wants an embedded software test engineer who can speak C firmware testing, medical-device lifecycle language (IEC 62304, ISO 14971), and Bluetooth Low Energy. She already holds the core skills (C/C++, embedded C, FreeRTOS, test automation, V&V); the plan fills BLE, regulatory vocabulary, and a build-now BLE firmware test project, with honest framing for the two structural gaps: 2+ years of embedded testing experience and implantable-device domain experience.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| C, C++, C#, Python | Have | "Experience with C, C++, C# and/or Python is required" |
| Unit/integration & automated testing | Have | "Experience with unit- and integration-level testing and automated testing is recommended" (TDD, Test automation, NI TestStand, LabVIEW registered) |
| Source code management | Have | "source code management is recommended" (Git, Bitbucket) |
| Formal methodologies / Agile | Have | "formal software development methodologies" (Agile/Scrum, Jira) |
| Requirements, V&V, root-cause analysis | Have | "gathering, analyzing, and validating requirements", "root-cause analysis of failures" (V&V registered) |
| Embedded C, FreeRTOS, SPI/I2C/UART | Have | Foundation for "testing embedded software" (ESP32, Arduino, Elevator Control project) |
| Bluetooth Low Energy (protocol + testing) | Learnable | "testing Bluetooth Low Energy within implantable medical devices is desired" |
| IEC 62304 software lifecycle vocabulary | Learnable | Design reviews, requirement/interface specs, "moderate risk" activities signal a 62304 process |
| ISO 14971 risk & hazard analysis | Learnable | "writing, updating, developing and maintaining Hazard/Risk/Cyber Security analysis specifications" |
| Medical device cybersecurity (threat modeling) | Learnable | Same line: cyber security analysis specs |
| MISRA C / static analysis for firmware test | Learnable | Implied by "critical test components" in a cardiac-rhythm context |
| 2+ years testing embedded software | Structural | "Minimum 2 years of experience in testing embedded software" |
| Implantable medical device domain | Structural | "within implantable medical devices" — regulated production experience |
| Never-claim list (Kubernetes, Terraform, dbt, etc.) | Never-claim | Irrelevant to this JD; never asserted anywhere |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **BLE fundamentals.** GAP/GATT, services/characteristics, pairing/bonding, connection intervals. Resource: Bluetooth SIG's free "Bluetooth Low Energy Primer" (bluetooth.com). Self-check: explain in 5 minutes how a heart-rate service notifies a phone, and name three things that break BLE links.
2. **IEC 62304 lifecycle vocabulary.** Software safety classes A/B/C, the development/maintenance processes, SOUP. Resource: FDA's free "Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions" guidance (fda.gov). Self-check: sketch the 62304 V-model from requirements to verification on one page.
3. **ISO 14971 risk vocabulary.** Hazard, foreseeable sequence of events, hazard situation, harm, risk control. Resource: free overview chapter summaries from BSI/IMDRF sites. Self-check: write one hazard analysis row (hazard → sequence → harm → control) for a pacemaker losing BLE connection.
4. **MISRA C awareness.** What it is, why cardiac firmware uses it, common rules. Resource: "MISRA C:2012 guidelines" summary pages and cppcheck docs. Self-check: spot three MISRA violations in a 20-line C snippet you write yourself.
5. **Requirement and interface specification language.** Design inputs, acceptance criteria, traceability, design reviews — the JD's first bullet. Resource: FDA Design Control guidance (free PDF). Self-check: turn a one-line user need into two testable requirements with acceptance criteria.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **BLE testing hands-on.** nRF Connect / Wireshark BLE sniffing, notification timing, disconnection edge cases. Artefact: a written walkthrough with captures titled "How I tested a BLE GATT service: 10 cases including radio loss."
2. **C firmware unit testing with Unity + CMock (Ceedling).** Mocking hardware registers, testing state machines. Artefact: a small GitHub repo testing a FreeRTOS task with 15+ unit tests and coverage notes.
3. **Cybersecurity threat modeling for a BLE medical device.** STRIDE over the pairing/data path; AAMI TIR57 concepts. Artefact: a one-page threat model document for her build-now project.
4. **Static analysis in practice.** Run cppcheck with MISRA addon on embedded code, triage findings. Artefact: before/after report committed in the repo showing findings fixed or justified.
5. **Requirements traceability matrix (RTM).** Requirement → design element → test case → result, the JD's "requirement and interface specifications" work. Artefact: an RTM spreadsheet/Markdown for the project, linked in the repo README.

## Build-now project

She has no BLE project; the JD explicitly desires BLE testing. Spec (not built yet):
- Goal: a simulated cardiac telemetry node demonstrating production-grade firmware testing.
- Hardware/data: ESP32 (registered skill); synthetic RR-interval/heart-rate data stream, no real patient data.
- Stack: Embedded C, FreeRTOS, ESP-IDF BLE GATT server; Unity/CMock unit tests; cppcheck static analysis.
- Features: heart-rate service with notifications, connection supervision timeout handling, error-state LED/logging.
- Testing: unit tests for state machine and packet parsing; integration test scripted in Python (Bleak) that connects, streams, drops, reconnects.
- Docs: requirements spec, hazard analysis table (ISO 14971 format), RTM.
- CI: GitHub Actions running unit tests and static analysis on every push — a pipeline she built herself.
- Evaluation: 90%+ unit-test pass, zero unresolved static-analysis defects, integration script passes 10/10 runs.
- Deliverable: public repo with README walkthrough. Estimate: 40-50 hours over weeks 2-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **2 years embedded testing:** "My embedded testing has been project-based — the elevator control system and medical IoT platform — rather than two full years in industry, and I'd want to be measured on how quickly my test discipline closes that gap."
- **Implantable devices:** "I haven't worked inside an implantable-device program. I have learned the 62304/14971 framework and built a BLE firmware test project to practice it, and I know the domain rigor is exactly what I'd be joining Abbott to absorb."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before, and nothing from this plan is claimed now.

sources.title: Abbott Careers - Software Engineer II, CRM Cardiac Rhythm Management, Sunnyvale (Job 31162832)
Bluetooth SIG - Bluetooth Low Energy Primer
FDA - Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions
FDA - Design Control Guidance for Medical Device Manufacturers

limitations: The JD is a generic Software Engineer II posting; the actual Sunnyvale CRM team's toolchain (RTOS, test frameworks, BLE chipsets) is not public, so Tier 2 picks the most probable stack from the JD wording rather than confirmed internal tools.
Whether her project-based embedded testing satisfies the 'minimum 2 years' requirement depends on the recruiter's screening; the plan cannot determine that, only prepare an honest answer.

Free resources named are the standard public entry points; IEC 62304 and ISO 14971 full standards are paywalled, so the plan relies on FDA guidance and public summaries rather than the standards text.
The build-now hour estimate (40-50h) is a planning figure, not a measured one.

plan.summary: Nuro's Onboard Platform role probes C++ systems depth she largely has, but will test profiling/tracing tooling (perf, Perfetto, Nsight), ROS-style robotics frameworks, GPU compute, and performance-tuning practice she does not yet have; the plan fronts those in weeks 1-5 with concrete proof artefacts. The structural gap is the '2+ years of relevant industry experience' line, which she must answer honestly from her embedded/FPGA project work.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill the JD names | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Strong C++ | Have | "Must have strong C++ skills" — registered |
| Python / advanced algorithms | Have | "advanced algorithms using C++ and Python" — registered |
| Highly-concurrent, multi-threaded environments | Have | "highly-concurrent, multi-processor, and multi-threaded environments" — Multithreading registered |
| Operating systems / Linux, real-time | Have | "computer architecture and operating systems" — Linux, FreeRTOS registered |
| Robotics hardware, sensors, embedded platforms | Have | "robotics hardware components (including sensors, embedded platforms)" — Embedded C, ESP32, SPI/I2C/UART, PID control registered; FPGA Autonomous Vehicle and Elevator Control projects |
| FPGA / ARM / x86 compute modalities | Have (FPGA/ARM) | "different compute modalities (x86, ARM, GPU, FPGA)" — Xilinx Vivado, Verilog, MicroBlaze registered |
| Profiling & tracing tools (perf, eBPF, Perfetto, pprof, Nsight) | Missing, learnable | "profiling and tracing tools and infrastructure" — none registered |
| Software performance tuning & optimization | Missing, learnable | "software performance tuning and optimization" — core to the Performance team |
| Robotics software frameworks (ROS 2 / DDS) | Missing, learnable | "robotics software frameworks" — none registered |
| GPU compute (CUDA, Nsight profiling) | Missing, learnable | "compute modalities ... GPU"; "NVIDIA Nsight Systems/Compute" |
| Large-scale distributed systems | Concepts learnable; production scale structural | "large-scale distributed systems" — she has Kafka/Spark data systems but not onboard/vehicle-scale production work |
| 2+ years relevant industry experience | Missing, structural | "2+ years of relevant industry experience in addition to a Bachelor's Degree" |
| CS/EE/Robotics degree | Have | MS (University of Arkansas) — a degree is never a gap |
| React | Not demanded by this JD; also on never-claim list — ignore for this role | n/a |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Profiling vocabulary: perf and flame graphs.** The JD names perf and pprof explicitly. Learn what sampling profilers measure (on-CPU vs off-CPU time). Resource: Brendan Gregg's free perf examples page (brendangregg.com/perf.html). Self-check: in 30 minutes, explain aloud what a flame graph's width and stack depth mean and where perf's overhead comes from.
2. **Tracing basics: Perfetto and eBPF.** The JD lists both. Learn trace events vs sampling, and what eBPF programs can hook (syscalls, uprobes). Resource: perfetto.dev "Quickstart: record traces on Linux". Self-check: describe in 30 minutes how you'd trace a latency spike in a sensor pipeline and which tool you'd pick first.
3. **ROS 2 core model.** "Robotics software frameworks" almost certainly means ROS 2 with DDS under it. Learn nodes, topics, pub/sub, QoS, launch. Resource: docs.ros.org Humble "Beginner: CLI tools" tutorials. Self-check: whiteboard a camera-driver -> perception -> planning topic graph in 30 minutes, naming message types.
4. **GPU execution model.** Learn threads/blocks/warps, memory hierarchy, occupancy — enough to discuss "GPU" as a compute modality. Resource: NVIDIA's free "CUDA C++ Programming Guide", chapters 1-3. Self-check: explain in 30 minutes why a naive matrix multiply is memory-bound and what tiling fixes.
5. **Real-time latency vocabulary.** The Performance team owns "latency reduction". Learn priority inversion, preemption, deadline vs throughput thinking. Resource: the Linux Foundation's free "Intro to Real-Time Linux" reading (wiki.linuxfoundation.org/realtime). Self-check: in 30 minutes, give three concrete causes of jitter in an onboard pipeline and one mitigation each.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Perf + flame-graph lab on her own C++ code.** Take an existing C++ project, find one hot loop, fix it, measure again. Artefact: a small repo with before/after flame-graph SVGs and a README walkthrough of the diagnosis.
2. **Perfetto-instrumented pipeline.** Instrument a multi-threaded producer/consumer pipeline with trace events. Artefact: repo plus two trace screenshots with a one-page written analysis of where latency hides.
3. **ROS 2 mini onboard pipeline.** Two C++ nodes (simulated sensor publisher, consumer with processing), measured end-to-end latency under load. Artefact: repo with a latency histogram and a note on how QoS settings changed it.
4. **CUDA kernel study.** Naive vs tiled matrix multiply, profiled. Artefact: notebook/repo with runtime table and, if hardware allows, Nsight Compute output; otherwise nvprof-style timing plus explanation of the bottleneck.
5. **Cache/SIMD optimization walkthrough.** Optimize one numerical kernel (row-major vs column-major access, compiler auto-vectorization). Artefact: written walkthrough with benchmark numbers and Compiler Explorer links showing the generated assembly.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

Her projects are hardware/FPGA-side; she has no software robotics-framework project. Spec (**not built yet**):
- Goal: simulate an onboard sensor-to-decision pipeline like the Onboard Systems team runs.
- Data: synthetic camera-frame and IMU streams generated in-process (no dataset needed).
- Stack: C++17, ROS 2 Humble, DDS pub/sub, Perfetto tracing, perf for profiling.
- Behavior: driver node -> preprocessing node -> mock perception node, each with a latency budget.
- Evaluation: end-to-end p50/p99 latency under increasing load; one documented optimization that cuts p99.
- Deliverable: public repo with README, trace screenshots, flame graphs, and the latency report.
- Hours: ~40 over weeks 3-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- "2+ years of relevant industry experience": "I'm earlier in my industry career than the posting describes, but I've built real-time and autonomous systems end to end — an FPGA-based autonomous vehicle and embedded control systems — and I can show you profiled, measured C++ work from the last month. I'd rather demonstrate the depth than claim the years."
- "Large-scale distributed systems": "My production-scale experience is in data systems — Kafka, Spark, Flink pipelines — not vehicle fleets. The concepts transfer and I've been studying onboard architectures, but I won't pretend I've debugged a fleet-wide deployment."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after each skill is actually learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

Perfetto — Quickstart: Record traces on Linux
ROS 2 Humble — Beginner: CLI tools tutorials

limitations: The JD does not name its exact robotics framework; ROS 2/DDS is the industry-standard inference for this role, but Nuro may run a proprietary middleware, in which case the concepts still transfer while specific tool names would not.
No access to Nuro's actual interview loop; tier contents are inferred from JD wording, not from confirmed interviewer behavior.
GPU hands-on work (Nsight Compute) depends on her having NVIDIA hardware; a fallback timing-only approach is noted but is weaker.
The 40-hour build project assumes she can carve out 8-10 hours per week; if the screening call comes earlier than week 3, Tier 2 items should be re-prioritized.

plan.summary: Twitch will probe whether she can talk like a data-platform engineer about petabyte-scale, highly available pipelines while staying honest that her evidence is streaming/ML projects rather than production ownership of a 200B-events/day system. The plan prioritizes data modeling, API/scalability vocabulary, AWS data-platform patterns, Kafka/Flink depth, and Go basics as learn-only because Go is never-claim.
plan.report:
## Demand map
| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Bachelor's CS or equivalent | Have | 'Bachelor's degree... or equivalent'; education is present and a held degree is never a gap. |
| Python | Have | Bonus 'Golang or Python'; Python is registered. |
| AWS | Have | Bonus 'Amazon Web Services'; registered EC2/S3/RDS/EMR/Glue/Lambda cover vocabulary. |
| Streaming/distributed compute evidence | Have | '200 billion events a day' maps to registered Kafka/Flink/Spark and the IoT analytics project. |
| Scalability, concurrency, distributed-systems fundamentals | Missing but learnable | Must-have 'Familiarity with scalability, concurrency... distributed systems'; she has parts, not crisp interview language. |
| API design | Missing but learnable | Must-have names 'API design'; no registered REST/gRPC term and gRPC is never-claim. |
| Data modeling | Missing but learnable | Must-have and the genuine gap; needed for 'data warehouses and pipelines'. |
| AI coding tools | Missing but learnable | 'Enhance our workflows using AI tooling' and 'Familiarity with AI coding tools'; adjacent GenAI skills exist, workflow evidence is thin. |
| Golang | Never-claim | Bonus 'Golang'; learn enough to compare tradeoffs, never say she has it. |
| Highly available production ownership at Twitch scale | Missing and structural | 'receives over 200 billion events a day' and 'next petabyte' imply years of operating blast radius she cannot fake. |
| Open-source contributions | Missing but learnable | Bonus; small docs/tests PRs are feasible, not a resume claim yet. |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)
1. Data modeling for warehouses: learn star schema, facts/dimensions, SCDs, partitioning vs clustering. Resource: Kimball dimensional modeling techniques summary. Self-check: sketch events, users, streams, games for Twitch chat and defend grain in 5 sentences.
2. API design fundamentals: resource naming, pagination, idempotency, versioning, errors, rate limits. Resource: freeCodeCamp 'REST API Best Practices' or Microsoft REST guidance. Self-check: design 'GET /channels/{id}/metrics' and explain 429/ETag choices.
3. Scalability vocabulary: horizontal scaling, backpressure, sharding, hotspots, exactly-once vs at-least-once. Resource: Kafka documentation design section. Self-check: explain how a partition key can create a hot shard during a big stream.
4. Concurrency fundamentals: threads vs async, locks, queues, backpressure, tail latency. Resource: Python concurrency docs plus her registered Multithreading as base. Self-check: describe a producer-consumer pipeline and where p99 blows up.
5. AI coding tools workflow: use Copilot-style tools for tests, refactors, docs while verifying output. Resource: GitHub Copilot docs/prompting guide. Self-check: state one rule she uses to catch plausible-but-wrong generated code.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)
1. Twitch-shaped AWS lakehouse: rehearse S3/Glue/EMR/Lambda patterns without claiming Redshift/Kinesis. Artefact: one-page architecture walkthrough for ingest -> raw S3 -> curated tables -> dashboards with failure modes.
2. Kafka depth beyond usage: partitions, consumer groups, ISR, retention, rebalancing, DLQ. Artefact: notebook or repo `kafka-notes` with a tiny local producer/consumer and rebalancing experiment.
3. Flink depth for live decisions: windows, watermarks, state, checkpoints, exactly-once sinks. Artefact: PyFlink/Flink SQL mini-demo counting events per streamer with late data, plus README on checkpoint recovery.
4. Data-warehouse modeling lab: model Twitch-like events into fact tables and incremental loads using Databricks/Delta Lake or SQL she has. Artefact: GitHub repo with schema diagram, DDL, sample queries, and tests for duplicate/out-of-order events.
5. Go comparison literacy only: learn syntax, goroutines, channels, why infra teams pick Go. Resource: A Tour of Go. Artefact: short written comparison 'Python service vs Go service for a metrics API' marked learning notes, not experience.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)
Not required: the JD reacts to existing registered Kafka/Flink/Spark/AWS plus the 'Real-Time Medical IoT Analytics Platform'. Extend that project instead: goal, replay 1M synthetic live events; data, JSON chat/viewer events; stack, Python, Kafka/Flink SQL, S3-compatible local store, Glue-style catalog notes; evaluation, end-to-end latency, duplicate rate, recovery after kill; deliverable, repo with README and Grafana screenshot; hours, 18-24; label: not built yet.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps
- Scale: 'I have built streaming analytics projects with Kafka/Flink and AWS services, but I have not operated a platform at 200 billion events per day; I am ready to learn that ownership from senior engineers.'
- Go: 'Python is my working language; I am studying Go because platform teams use it, but I would not present myself as a Go engineer yet.'

## When this may go on the resume
Only after a topic is learned, proven by an artefact, written into data/context/, and then re-registered; never before.

plan.summary: Upstart's Lifecycle Platform role is a strong match on streaming and data fundamentals (Kafka, Flink, Spark, AWS, Python/Java are all registered), but the JD's marketing-platform layer — CDPs, campaign orchestration, reverse ETL — is entirely new territory and is what interviewers will probe. Airbyte and Fivetran are never-claim: learn the concepts, never list them. The plan front-loads lifecycle-messaging vocabulary for the screen, then builds one event-triggered messaging repo as proof before the technical round.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python / Java | Have | "Proficiency in at least one backend language such as Kotlin, Java, Ruby, or Python" |
| AWS (EC2, S3, Lambda, Glue, RDS) | Have | "microservices and APIs in a cloud environment (preferably AWS)" |
| Kafka / Flink / Spark, real-time streaming | Have | "real-time event streaming systems and high-throughput messaging architectures" |
| Databricks, ETL/ELT, SQL | Have | "data pipeline tooling (e.g., Airbyte, Fivetran, Databricks)" |
| Docker, CI/CD, Flask, TDD | Have | "Design and build scalable backend services… deploy frequently" |
| Kotlin | Learnable | Listed first among backend languages; trivial hop from Java |
| Microservices & API system design | Learnable | Core of the role; probe depth beyond her project scale |
| CDPs, customer segmentation, campaign orchestration | Learnable | "particularly in environments involving CDPs, customer segmentation, or campaign orchestration" |
| Reverse ETL (Hightouch/Census concept) | Learnable | "reverse ETL workflows" named in impact section |
| Messaging channels: email/SMS/push deliverability | Learnable | Team owns "preference management, email, SMS, push notifications" |
| Marketing automation platforms (Iterable, Braze, SFMC) | Learnable | Named preferred tools; concepts matter more than the GUI |
| 3+ yrs production SWE + leading medium projects | Structural | "3 years of experience… Lead medium-sized projects independently" |
| Supporting Marketing/Growth/GTM teams | Structural | Preferred: "Experience supporting Marketing, Growth, or GTM teams" |
| Airbyte, Fivetran | Never-claim | In never_claim_skills; learn the category, never assert hands-on |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Lifecycle marketing & CDP vocabulary.** Learn what a CDP does, identity resolution, segmentation, and the difference between campaign orchestration and transactional messaging. Resource: Segment's free "CDP guide" (segment.com/resources) plus Iterable's blog glossary. Self-check: explain in 5 minutes, unaided, how customer data flows from product events to an email send, naming each stage.
2. **Reverse ETL concept.** Learn what reverse ETL is, why warehouses push data back to SaaS tools, and where Hightouch/Census fit — conceptually, since Airbyte/Fivetran are never-claim. Resource: Hightouch's free "What is Reverse ETL?" guide. Self-check: draw a reverse-ETL diagram on paper and contrast it with classic ETL in two sentences each.
3. **Email/SMS/push fundamentals.** Deliverability, opt-in/opt-out and preference management, provider APIs (Twilio, SendGrid, FCM/APNs). Resource: Twilio's free Messaging docs and SendGrid's deliverability guide. Self-check: answer "why can a 'sent' email never arrive?" with at least four distinct reasons.
4. **Kotlin crash pass.** Syntax, null safety, coroutines at reading level — enough to say "Java-daily, Kotlin-readable." Resource: official Kotlin Koans (kotlinlang.org). Self-check: complete 10 Koans and rewrite one small Java class in Kotlin.
5. **Her honest position script.** For each must-have, one sentence: what she's built, what she's learning. Self-check: record herself answering "walk me through your microservices experience" in 90 seconds without overclaiming.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Event-triggered messaging pipeline.** Kafka consumer in Python that triggers templated "email/SMS" sends (mocked providers), with idempotency and retry logic. Artefact: public GitHub repo with README architecture diagram and docker-compose one-command run.
2. **Reverse ETL walkthrough.** Model customer segments in PostgreSQL, write a small Python sync that pushes a segment to a mock destination API with diffing and rate limits. Artefact: Jupyter notebook + written walkthrough titled "Reverse ETL, from scratch, no vendor tools."
3. **Marketing-platform API study.** Read Iterable's and Braze's public REST docs; map their objects (users, events, campaigns, journeys) to a generic schema. Artefact: one-page comparison doc she can discuss — shows domain fluency without claiming production use.
4. **Notification-platform system design.** Design Upstart's unified comms platform on paper: ingestion, preferences, scheduling, per-channel workers, observability. Resource: "System Design Interview" (Alex Xu) notification chapter + AWS SQS/SNS docs. Artefact: written design doc with trade-offs section, rehearsed as a 30-minute whiteboard answer.
5. **Experimentation/messaging-analytics depth.** How A/B tests on messaging are measured (holdout groups, conversion attribution) since JD says "experimentation capabilities." Artefact: short notebook simulating a holdout-group lift calculation on synthetic send data.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

Needed — no messaging/marketing-automation project exists. **Not built yet.**
- Goal: miniature lifecycle-messaging platform proving the JD's core loop: events in, right message out.
- Data: synthetic user events (signups, purchases) generated by a Python producer.
- Stack: Python + Kafka + PostgreSQL (preferences/segments) + mocked SendGrid/Twilio adapters; Docker Compose; GitHub Actions CI.
- Features: preference management (opt in/out per channel), one event-triggered journey (welcome series), one segment-triggered batch campaign.
- Evaluation: idempotent delivery under consumer restarts; unit tests for preference logic; end-to-end test event → mock send.
- Deliverable: repo + README with architecture diagram + 5-minute Loom walkthrough.
- Hours: ~35 over weeks 2-4.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- "My professional background is in data and ML engineering — about X years — not three years of pure product-backend work; what transfers directly is building and operating streaming pipelines and APIs in production on AWS."
- "I haven't supported a marketing org before, but I've sat with non-engineering stakeholders to turn fuzzy requirements into shipped pipelines; the CDP and campaign-orchestration domain is what I've been deliberately studying for this role."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after it is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered.
limitations: Current Upstart production stack details beyond the JD wording (e.g., exact languages in the Lifecycle team) were not verified; Tier 2 items target the JD's stated stack.
Interview format at Upstart (screening vs. technical round structure) is assumed from standard SWE II loops, not confirmed.
Registered skills are treated as genuine per instructions; the plan does not re-validate their depth, so some 'Have' buckets may still need refresh before interviews.

plan.summary: The Block Financial Platform role is strongest where she already has depth (Kafka, Java, Python, AWS, ETL) and gaps cluster in gRPC, workflow-engine design, financial-domain vocabulary, and the JD's named tools Kubernetes and Snowflake — the last two learnable but never claimable. The plan front-loads finance and workflow vocabulary plus idempotency/audit fundamentals for the screening call, then builds two proof artefacts (an event-driven ledger service and a migration design doc) before the technical round.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Java, Python | Have | "Languages: Kotlin, Java, Python, JavaScript" |
| Apache Kafka, event-driven architectures | Have | "event streams, and messaging patterns" for integrations |
| AWS (EC2, S3, Lambda, Glue), MySQL, REST APIs, CI/CD, Docker | Have | "Infrastructure: AWS", "Data: MySQL", "APIs and integrations" |
| ETL/pipelines, operational analytics | Have | "building data pipelines or reporting systems" (nice to have) |
| Prompt engineering, LangChain, local LLMs | Have (adjacent) | "AI-first mentality", but JD means agentic coding tools specifically |
| Financial vocabulary: GL, reconciliation, revenue, FP&A, tax | Missing, learnable | "from revenue streams to reconciliations to GL to street reporting" |
| Workflow/state-machine systems | Missing, learnable | "configurable workflow engines, rules-based routing… human-in-the-loop steps" |
| Idempotency, audit trails, access controls by default | Missing, learnable | "audit trails, access controls, and data governance baked in" |
| Platform migration patterns | Missing, learnable | "migration of business-critical workflows… zero disruption during cutover" |
| Agentic engineering: Claude Code, Goose, MCP | Missing, learnable | "Direct AI agents across the full development lifecycle" |
| Kotlin, DynamoDB, Prometheus/DataDog, LaunchDarkly | Missing, learnable | Listed under "Technologies We Use and Teach" |
| gRPC / Protocol Buffers | Never-claim (learn, don't claim) | "Protocols: HTTP, JSON, gRPC, Protocol Buffers" |
| Kubernetes | Never-claim (learn, don't claim) | "Infrastructure: AWS, Kubernetes" |
| Snowflake | Never-claim (learn, don't claim) | "Data: DynamoDB, MySQL, Kafka, Snowflake" |
| 6+ years on complex systems | Structural | "6+ working on complex systems and delivering quality software" |
| Financial-services production background | Structural | "Experience working on financially sensitive or regulated systems" |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Finance platform vocabulary** — the JD's "revenue streams to reconciliations to GL". Learn double-entry basics, what a general ledger is, what reconciliation means. Resource: Khan Academy "Accounting and financial statements" (free). Self-check: in 30 min, explain on paper how a Square seller payment flows from revenue event to GL entry to a reconciled report, and where it could break.
2. **Workflow/state machines** — the JD's "entities move through complex lifecycles with branching logic, SLAs, and human-in-the-loop steps". Resource: Temporal's free "Temporal 101" course docs. Self-check: model an invoice-approval lifecycle (states, transitions, SLA timers, human escalation) as a state diagram without notes.
3. **Idempotency and audit trails** — the JD says these matter "by default". Resource: AWS Builders' Library article "Making retries safe with idempotent APIs" (free). Self-check: sketch an idempotent ledger-write endpoint (idempotency keys, dedup window, immutable audit log) and explain why retries can't double-post.
4. **gRPC + Protocol Buffers (never-claim)** — named in "Protocols". Resource: official grpc.io "Introduction to gRPC" and "Basics tutorial" for Python (free). Self-check: write a small .proto for a ledger service with one unary and one streaming RPC; explain gRPC vs REST trade-offs. Honest line if asked: "I've studied it and built a toy service; I haven't run it in production."
5. **Agentic engineering: Claude Code, Goose, MCP** — the JD's core culture signal ("we expect every engineer to do the same"). She has LangChain/prompt engineering; this is the applied version. Resource: Block's open-source Goose docs (block.github.io/goose) and Anthropic's MCP introduction (free). Self-check: run Goose locally on a small repo task and describe, in 3 sentences, how she'd review and own agent-written code.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Event-driven ledger service** — directly mirrors "backend services… with audit trails". Build a double-entry ledger API in Python or Java: Kafka events, idempotent writes, MySQL, append-only audit table, access checks. Artefact: public GitHub repo with README architecture diagram and tests proving no double-posting under retries.
2. **Platform migration design** — the JD's "Lead a platform migration… zero disruption". Study strangler-fig pattern, dual-writes, backfill, phased rollout, feature flags (LaunchDarkly's free tier). Artefact: a written design doc (repo or gist): "Migrating a vendor reconciliation workflow to an internal system" with cutover plan, rollback, and flag strategy.
3. **DynamoDB data modeling** — named under "Data"; her AWS base makes this fast. Resource: AWS's free "Amazon DynamoDB deep dive" on YouTube/AWS Skill Builder. Artefact: notebook or repo modeling chart-of-accounts access patterns with single-table design, GSIs, and rationale.
4. **Snowflake (never-claim)** — named under "Data". Learn via Snowflake's free 30-day trial + official Quickstart "Getting Started with Snowflake". Artefact: notebook loading sample finance data, running window-function reconciliation queries. Learned, never claimed on the resume.
5. **Kubernetes + observability (K8s never-claim)** — "Infrastructure: AWS, Kubernetes"; "DataDog, Prometheus". Resource: official kubernetes.io tutorials with minikube, plus Prometheus "Getting started" (free). Artefact: short written walkthrough deploying her existing Flask expense-tracker API to minikube with a Prometheus metrics endpoint. Learned, never claimed.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has no workflow-engine project; the JD centers on one. Spec — **"not built yet"**:
- Goal: configurable rules-based workflow engine for invoice approvals.
- Data: synthetic invoices (generated with Pandas) across 3 fake business units.
- Stack: Python, Flask, MySQL, Kafka; states persisted; SLAs as timers.
- Features: YAML-defined state machines per BU, branching rules, human-in-the-loop queue UI, SLA breach events, full audit log.
- Evaluation: replay 10k events; show no lost transitions, audit completeness, latency under load.
- Deliverable: GitHub repo + README with state diagrams and a demo script.
- Hours: ~30-40, fits inside Tier 2 weeks 3-5 alongside item 1.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- On "6+ years": "I have fewer years than the posting asks, but I've built and operated distributed streaming systems end-to-end — Kafka, Flink, Airflow — and I'd rather show you the ledger service I built for this process than claim years I don't have."
- On regulated/financial systems: "I haven't shipped inside a regulated finance org yet. I've studied why idempotency, audit trails, and retention matter and built them into my own services — I'm looking for the environment where those defaults are non-negotiable."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is actually learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — and Kubernetes, Snowflake, and gRPC stay off it regardless, per her never-claim list.

plan.summary: Roku's Content Ingestion role is a cloud/DevOps-heavy ingestion-pipeline job; she already covers Python, AWS, Docker, Kafka, Postgres/MongoDB, Grafana, CI/CD and Linux, so the plan targets the real gaps: Bash scripting, GCP, Ansible, Prometheus, caching/scaling concepts, and the agentic toolchain story. Terraform and Kubernetes are never-claim skills — she can learn and build with them now but may not list them until they are learned, built into data/context/, and re-registered.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python, C++ | Have | "Proficiency in one or more of: Python, Bash, C++, or Go" |
| AWS (EC2, S3, RDS, Glue, Lambda) | Have | "cloud platforms such as AWS and/or GCP" |
| Docker, Git, CI/CD, Linux | Have | "Manage containerized deployments… CI/CD pipelines and version control via Git" |
| Kafka, Postgres, MongoDB, Grafana | Have | "message queues… relational (Postgres) and non-relational (MongoDB)… Prometheus and Grafana" |
| Flask (APIs), ETL/ELT, Airflow | Have | "APIs and batch jobs for asset ingestion, processing, and distribution" |
| LangChain, prompt engineering | Have (partial) | "agentic AI workflows within active code repositories" |
| Bash scripting | Learnable (wk 1-2) | Named first in the language list; "strong foundation in… scripting" |
| GCP fundamentals | Learnable (wk 2-5) | "full-stack operations across cloud and on-premises… AWS and GCP" |
| Ansible | Learnable (wk 2-5) | "infrastructure… using Terraform and Ansible" |
| Prometheus + Alertmanager | Learnable (wk 2-5) | "monitoring, alerting, and observability using… Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager" |
| Caching strategies, horizontal/vertical scaling | Learnable (wk 1-2) | "Understanding of message queues, caching strategies, and horizontal/vertical scaling" |
| ACR / content-ingestion domain | Learnable (wk 1-2) | "real-time content matching… for Roku's ACR platform" |
| MCP servers, agentic coding harness fluency | Learnable (wk 2-5) | "coding harnesses like Claude Code or Cursor, MCP servers, custom skills" |
| Terraform | Never-claim (learn only) | "Create and manage infrastructure… using Terraform" |
| Kubernetes | Never-claim (learn only) | "Manage containerized deployments using Docker and Kubernetes" |
| Go | Never-claim (skip — Python/C++ satisfy the list) | one-of language list |
| 1-3 years professional experience | Structural | "1–3 years of hands-on engineering experience" |
| On-call for critical production services | Structural | "participating in on-call rotations" — she has no production on-call history |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Bash scripting fundamentals** — pipes, exit codes, cron, writing a log-parsing script. Resource: *The Linux Command Line* (free PDF, linuxcommand.org). Self-check: in 30 min, write a script that tails a log, counts 5xx errors per minute, and alerts over a threshold — no notes.
2. **Scaling & caching vocabulary** — horizontal vs vertical scaling, cache-aside vs write-through, where Redis/CDN caches sit (concept only; Redis is never-claim as a skill). Resource: ByteByteGo's free "Scaling 101" articles/newsletter. Self-check: whiteboard aloud in 30 min how an ingestion API handling "millions of assets" scales from 1 to 100 machines.
3. **ACR and content-ingestion domain** — what Automatic Content Recognition is, how linear-feed fingerprinting works, what "asset ingestion" means for a streaming platform. Resource: Roku's own engineering blog (engineering.roku.com) plus the ACR Wikipedia overview. Self-check: explain in 2 minutes, out loud, what the Content Ingestion team produces and who consumes it.
4. **Message-queue depth beyond Kafka usage** — consumer groups, idempotency, dead-letter queues, backpressure, framed as ingestion concerns. Resource: Kafka's free official design docs. Self-check: in 30 min, write one page on how she'd make a partner-file ingestion job exactly-once.
5. **Honest-status script** — one sentence per missing tool stating where she is ("learning Ansible this month, built X with it"). Self-check: say each one without apologizing or inflating.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **GCP core services mapped from AWS knowledge** — GCE≈EC2, GCS≈S3, Cloud SQL≈RDS, Pub/Sub≈Kafka-lite. Resource: Google Cloud Skills Boost free tier. Artefact: a written side-by-side migration walkthrough of her IoT analytics platform from AWS to GCP (markdown doc in a repo).
2. **Ansible for instance setup** — playbooks, roles, inventory, idempotent config. Resource: Jeff Geerling's free *Ansible for DevOps* (early chapters) and docs.ansible.com. Artefact: a repo with a playbook that provisions an Ubuntu VM with Docker, Postgres, and her ingestion app.
3. **Prometheus + Alertmanager on top of her Grafana knowledge** — metrics types, PromQL basics, alert rules, PagerDuty-style routing. Resource: prometheus.io docs + free "Prometheus Up & Running" excerpts. Artefact: a docker-compose demo where her Flask API exports metrics, Prometheus scrapes, Alertmanager fires a rule; screenshot + README.
4. **Agentic toolchain story** — the JD explicitly probes "MCP servers, custom skills… verify its output." Resource: Anthropic's free MCP documentation. Artefact: a short written walkthrough of driving an agent on an unfamiliar open-source repo, with verification steps she ran.
5. **On-call & observability literacy** — SLOs, error budgets, runbooks, incident retros. Resource: Google SRE book free chapters (sre.google). Artefact: a mock runbook for her demo pipeline, including alert thresholds and rollback steps.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

**Not built yet.** The JD runs Kubernetes/Terraform and she has no such project. Spec: **partner content-ingestion mini-platform**. Goal: simulate a content partner dropping metadata/video-manifest files; ingest, validate, store, expose status API. Data: synthetic asset manifests (JSON, ~10k records, seeded errors). Stack: Python + Flask API, Postgres, Docker, Terraform (localstack or free-tier AWS) for infra, Minikube for Kubernetes deployment, Prometheus+Grafana for monitoring. Evaluation: pipeline survives a killed pod, rejects malformed manifests, dashboard shows ingest rate and error alerts. Deliverable: public repo with README, architecture diagram, and a 5-minute demo video. ~40 hours across weeks 2-5. This stays off the resume until built and re-registered — Terraform/Kubernetes are never-claim until then.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **1-3 years experience:** "I'm early-career — my experience is project and research based, including building streaming and ETL platforms end to end. I'm upfront that I haven't held a multi-year production role yet, and I'm looking for exactly this kind of team to grow in."
- **On-call:** "I haven't been on a production on-call rotation, but I've studied SRE practices and built alerting into my own projects — I take ownership seriously and I'm ready to carry a pager."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: Upstart's Distribution Platform role matches most of her registered depth (Python/Java, AWS, SQL, Kafka-scale data systems); the plan focuses on Ruby/Rails or Kotlin, React/TypeScript, and ad-platform/marketing-tech fluency. The only structural gap is the '3 years of experience' requirement, with honest-answer scripts provided.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python / Java ('Strong proficiency in one or more programming languages') | Have | Core language bar |
| Scalable APIs & microservices on cloud ('Experience building scalable APIs and microservices in a cloud-based environment (e.g., AWS)') | Have | Team builds serving systems |
| 3rd-party integrations / large data ('integrate with 3rd parties and/or ingest, store, expose large amounts of data') | Have | Partner integrations, ads data |
| SQL / data warehouses ('Experience with SQL, data warehouses') | Have | Analytics collaboration |
| Bachelor's degree + 3 years experience | Structural | Minimum qualification; degree held, years are the gap |
| Ruby on Rails and/or Kotlin ('Professional experience with Ruby on Rails and/or Kotlin') | Missing, learnable | Their actual stack |
| React / TypeScript / front end ('Experience or interest in working with React, typescript, or front end technologies') | Never-claim (learnable now) | Occasional UI work on internal tools |
| Google Ads / Meta Ads ('Professional experience with digital advertising platforms') | Missing, learnable (knowledge); 'professional' part is structural | Highest-value channel is digital ads |
| Marketing tech / growth engineering ('Experience working with marketing technology or growth engineering') | Missing, learnable | Domain vocabulary for screening |
| Leading projects ('leading small to medium sized projects over multiple months') | Have | Multi-month project leadership in her history |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Marketing-tech vocabulary**: attribution, CAC/ROAS, conversion funnel, A/B testing, channel mix (digital ads, direct mail, partner integrations — the JD's own list). Resource: HubSpot Academy's free Digital Marketing course. Self-check: explain in 2 minutes how Upstart would measure a direct-mail campaign's lift.
2. **Ruby fundamentals**: syntax, blocks, gems, irb fluency. Resource: The Odin Project's Ruby course (free). Self-check: write a small CLI script parsing a CSV without looking up syntax.
3. **Google Ads platform basics**: campaigns, ad groups, bidding, the API's shape. Resource: Google Skillshop's free Google Ads courses. Self-check: whiteboard how you'd sync audience segments to Google Ads nightly.
4. **Rails mental model**: MVC, routing, ActiveRecord, migrations. Resource: official Rails Guides (guides.rubyonrails.org). Self-check: sketch the request lifecycle for 'GET /campaigns/:id' from memory.
5. **Upstart domain prep**: lending marketplace, AI underwriting, why distribution efficiency matters to unit economics. Resource: Upstart's engineering blog (upstart.com/engineering). Self-check: give a 90-second answer to 'why this team?' citing the JD's 'right users with the right content at the right time'.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Rails API depth**: build a CRUD JSON API with PostgreSQL, background job, and tests. Artefact: public GitHub repo with README and request examples.
2. **React + TypeScript basics** (never-claim until re-registered): components, hooks, typed props, fetching from the Rails API. Artefact: a small typed frontend repo consuming that API.
3. **Third-party integration patterns**: OAuth, webhooks, rate limits, retry with backoff, idempotency — directly relevant to 'integrate with 3rd parties'. Artefact: a repo that ingests a public API (e.g., ad-report-style CSV/JSON) into Postgres with retries and a written design note.
4. **Experimentation analytics**: A/B test design, significance, reading marketing data with SQL. Artefact: a Jupyter notebook analyzing a public marketing dataset with SQL + Pandas, ending in a go/no-go recommendation.
5. **Content-serving system design**: low-latency decisioning, caching, feature flags, audience targeting at scale. Artefact: a written one-page design walkthrough of 'serve the right content to the right user' with trade-offs.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has no web/full-stack service project of this type, so: **AdServe-lite (not built yet)**.
- Goal: miniature marketing-content serving service, mirroring the team's problem.
- Data: synthetic user/audience segments and creative metadata generated with Faker.
- Stack: Rails API + PostgreSQL + Redis-free in-memory cache; React/TypeScript admin UI; Docker Compose; deployed on AWS (EC2 or Lambda).
- Features: audience rules engine, per-user content decisioning endpoint, event logging to Postgres, simple A/B assignment.
- Evaluation: p95 latency < 50ms locally; unit tests for the rules engine; an experiment-results SQL query.
- Deliverable: GitHub repo, architecture diagram, 5-minute Loom walkthrough.
- Hours: ~40-50 over weeks 2-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- On '3 years of experience': "My experience is intensive and project-based rather than three years in industry — across my MS and multi-month team projects I've owned design, delivery, and collaboration end to end, and I'm confident ramping quickly on the parts that are new."
- On professional ad-platform experience: "I haven't run Google or Meta ads professionally yet — I've built the fundamentals through Skillshop and a demo campaign-serving service, so I understand the concepts and the API surface, and I'd be honest about where I'd need a teammate's review early on."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — nothing in this plan may be claimed before that.

plan.summary: This Block Payment Interfaces role demands production payments experience and 6-8+ years that cannot be learned in five weeks; the plan targets the learnable layer instead: payment-API vocabulary (idempotency, retries, partial failures), Kotlin and TypeScript fundamentals, and incident-response/SRE practices, anchored by a self-built idempotent payment API project. Kafka, AWS, CI/CD, and AI-assisted engineering are already Have; Go stays on the never-claim list even though the JD names it.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Apache Kafka | Have | "Technologies We Use and Teach: Kafka" |
| AWS (EC2, S3, Lambda, RDS, Glue) | Have | "Technologies We Use and Teach: AWS" |
| AI-assisted engineering | Have (LangChain, prompt engineering, local LLMs) | "Fluency with AI-assisted engineering tools... validate generated code" |
| CI/CD, Docker, TDD, design patterns | Have | "own testing, rollout", "automation to reduce repetitive operational work" |
| Payment API concerns: idempotency, retries, async processing, backward compatibility, partial failures | Learnable | "An understanding of payment API concerns such as idempotency, retries..." |
| Kotlin | Learnable (Java is Have; Kotlin is not registered) | "Technologies We Use and Teach: Kotlin" |
| TypeScript | Learnable (not registered) | "Technologies We Use and Teach: TypeScript" |
| Incident response, SLOs, postmortems | Learnable (Grafana is Have) | "on-call rotation, investigate incidents... preventive engineering" |
| Production payments experience | Structural | "Experience building, maintaining, and scaling customer-facing financial or payment APIs... This is a requirement" |
| High-volume production operation record | Structural | "high-volume, highly available distributed systems where correctness... matter" |
| 8 yrs + Bachelor's / 6 yrs + Master's | Structural (her Master's degree itself is never a gap) | "A minimum of 8 years of related experience with a Bachelor's degree; or 6 years and a Master's" |
| Go | Never-claim (may be learned later, never claimed) | "Technologies We Use and Teach: Go" |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Idempotency and retries.** The JD: "idempotency, retries... without compromising financial correctness." Learn idempotency-key lifecycle, safe retry semantics, exponential backoff with jitter. Resource: Stripe's idempotent-requests docs plus the AWS Builders' Library article "Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter." Self-check: explain on paper what happens when a POST /payments times out after the charge succeeded, and how the key prevents a double charge.
2. **Async processing, webhooks, backward compatibility.** The JD: "asynchronous processing, backward compatibility." Learn webhook delivery (at-least-once, signatures, DLQs) and additive-only API evolution. Resource: Stripe webhooks documentation. Self-check: sketch a v1-to-v2 change adding a field and argue why old clients never break.
3. **Kotlin for a Java developer.** The JD lists Kotlin first under technologies. Resource: kotlinlang.org "Java to Kotlin" migration guide and Kotlin docs on coroutines. Self-check: write a data class, a null-safe call chain, and one suspending function from memory.
4. **TypeScript basics.** Resource: The TypeScript Handbook (official). Self-check: type a JSON payment response and catch a deliberate type error.
5. **Incident response vocabulary.** The JD: "on-call rotation, investigate incidents." Learn SLOs, error budgets, blameless postmortems. Resource: Google SRE Book (free online), chapters on monitoring and postmortem culture. Self-check: write a one-page postmortem for an imaginary payments outage in 30 minutes.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **The build-now project below** — Artefact: public repo with README and design doc.
2. **Kafka correctness patterns.** Her Kafka is registered; go deeper into consumer-side idempotency, ordering, and dead-letter queues for financial events. Artefact: a demo that runs a duplicate-producer/retry storm and shows exactly-once-effect at the consumer, with a notebook of results.
3. **Distributed failure modes of payment systems.** Artefact: a written walkthrough (markdown, ~5 pages) of timeouts, partial failures, and reconciliation, each tied to a JD phrase — this doubles as interview prep.
4. **Observability for a payment API.** The JD: "improve performance, observability, fault tolerance." Artefact: Grafana dashboard (Grafana is Have) plus a written SLO: latency, error rate, duplicate-charge rate = 0.
5. **Kotlin backend in anger.** Artefact: the same repo from item 1, written in Kotlin — proof she can work in their primary language, stated honestly as "recently learned."

## Build-now project (she has no payment-API project)

**PayGate-mini — idempotent payment API (not built yet)**
- Goal: a small customer-facing payment API demonstrating every JD concern: idempotency, retries, async webhooks, partial-failure handling.
- Stack: Kotlin (Ktor), PostgreSQL (Have), Kafka (Have) for async events, Docker (Have), deployed on AWS free tier (Have). Flask/Python alternative acceptable if Kotlin slows her down.
- Features: POST /payments with idempotency keys; retry-safe client SDK; webhook dispatcher with DLQ; simulated downstream outage.
- Evaluation: a chaos test — kill the "processor" mid-request, fire duplicate requests — must produce zero double charges; results table in README.
- Deliverable: GitHub repo, README with architecture diagram and the Tier-2 walkthrough linked.
- Hours: ~35 over weeks 2-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **No production payments experience:** "I haven't run payment systems in production yet, and I won't pretend otherwise. I built PayGate-mini to learn the failure modes hands-on — idempotency, retries, reconciliation — and my streaming and data work taught me correctness under retries at volume. I know Block's scale is deeper, and that gap is exactly why I prepared this way."
- **Years of experience:** "I hold a Master's degree, so I read the requirement as six years. My years are in data, streaming, and embedded systems rather than payments specifically — distributed correctness transfers, the payments domain is what I'm learning now, and I'd rather be honest about that than oversell."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is actually learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — nothing in this plan is resume material today.

plan.summary: Point72's Macro Quant Analytics role is a C# distributed-systems job at heart, and her registered .NET/C#, Python, C++, Kafka, Docker and AWS background covers the core — the real prep work is gRPC, time-aware data modeling, Kubernetes familiarity, and rates/FX/derivatives vocabulary, none of which may go on the resume yet. This plan sequences vocabulary-first prep for the screening call, then artefact-backed depth for the technical round, plus honest scripts for the two structural gaps: years of production backend experience and finance domain exposure.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| C#, .NET backend ("production-quality backend software in C#") | Have | Core language for the macro analytics library |
| Python, C++ ("exposure to C++... performance- or analytics-oriented") | Have | Research tooling and performance-critical paths |
| Kafka, streaming pipelines ("streaming and messaging systems, such as Kafka") | Have | Real-time market data and derived data pipelines |
| Docker, AWS/cloud deployment ("cloud or hybrid environments") | Have | Service packaging and deployment |
| SQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, data modeling generally | Have | Persistence for historical analytics |
| Testing, CI/CD, monitoring ("SDLC best practices... code coverage, monitoring") | Have | Reliability of shared analytics platforms |
| Distributed-systems design ("consistency, time-series or event-driven architectures") | Have (fundamentals via Flink/Kafka/multithreading) | Correctness and latency guarantees |
| gRPC ("APIs (REST/gRPC)") | Never-claim — learn now, never list | Inter-service protocol the team standardizes on |
| Time-aware data modeling ("time-aware (historical and real-time) data models") | Missing, learnable in 3-6 weeks | Consistency across backtest vs. live analytics |
| Financial markets: rates, FX, derivatives ("how pricing and risk analytics are applied") | Missing, learnable in 3-6 weeks (vocabulary) | Partnering with quants and PMs |
| Kubernetes ("familiarity with containerized environments") | Never-claim — learn now, never list | Operating containerized services |
| 3-10 years production backend experience ("3-10 years of experience developing production-quality backend software") | Missing, structural | Seniority and judgment; cannot be compressed into weeks |
| Production finance/trading systems exposure | Missing, structural | Domain trust with investment professionals |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **gRPC fundamentals** (JD: "APIs (REST/gRPC)"). Learn: protobuf schemas, unary vs. streaming RPCs, deadlines, gRPC vs. REST trade-offs. Resource: Microsoft Learn "Introduction to gRPC on .NET" (free). Self-check: in 30 min, explain aloud when gRPC beats REST for internal analytics services and sketch a .proto for a price-quote stream.
2. **Time-series / event-driven design vocabulary** (JD: "time-series or event-driven architectures"). Learn: event time vs. processing time, bitemporal tables, watermarks, idempotent consumers. Resource: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" chapters 1-3 (free via many university libraries) plus Kafka docs on semantics. Self-check: whiteboard in 30 min how you'd keep a backtest dataset and a live feed consistent.
3. **Rates, FX, derivatives basics** (JD: "awareness of financial markets and instruments, including rates, FX, and derivatives"). Learn: what a swap, future, and FX forward are; what "pricing" and "risk" (Greeks, DV01) mean. Resource: Investopedia's free tutorials on swaps, FX forwards, and options Greeks. Self-check: in 30 min, explain DV01 and a vanilla interest-rate swap to a non-finance friend.
4. **Modern C# performance idioms** (JD: "high-performance distributed systems... latency"). Learn: Span<T>, Memory<T>, ArrayPool, async/await pitfalls, GC modes. Resource: Microsoft's free "Performance best practices with C#" talk/blog series on .NET. Self-check: explain in 30 min how you'd reduce allocations in a hot pricing loop.
5. **Kubernetes concepts only** (JD asks "familiarity" — learn, never claim). Learn: pods, deployments, services, configmaps, probes. Resource: kubernetes.io free "Kubernetes Basics" tutorial. Self-check: describe in 30 min what happens when a pod dies mid-request.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **gRPC service in C#** — build a small market-data server exposing unary and server-streaming RPCs. Artefact: GitHub repo with .proto files, a .NET server, and a README walkthrough of a latency benchmark vs. a REST equivalent.
2. **Time-aware data model** — design a bitemporal schema for tick data in ClickHouse or PostgreSQL (both already hers). Artefact: repo with DDL, sample ingest script, and a written note on as-of queries and why they matter for backtesting.
3. **Derived-data Kafka pipeline in C#** (JD: "derived data generation and persistence"). Artefact: repo where a C# consumer computes rolling VWAP from a raw-trade topic into a derived topic, with idempotent writes and a Grafana dashboard (Grafana is registered).
4. **Local Kubernetes deployment, labeled as learning** — deploy item 1's service to kind/minikube with probes and resource limits. Artefact: manifests plus a written walkthrough of a rolling update. Present it only as "I taught myself this," never as experience.
5. **Mini pricing/risk notebook in Python** (JD: "pricing, risk, and global market data workflows"). Artefact: Jupyter notebook pricing a bond and an FX forward, computing DV01 and simple Greeks, with plain-English commentary she could narrate to a PM.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

**Not built yet.** Goal: a C# "macro rates analytics service" mimicking this team's world — none of her projects are finance or time-aware analytics services. Data: free daily treasury yield-curve and FX rates (FRED/ECB CSVs). Stack: .NET 8, gRPC + REST endpoints, PostgreSQL bitemporal store, Kafka for derived curves, Docker. Scope: ingest historical series, serve as-of queries, compute derived forward curves. Evaluation: correctness checks against published curve math; p99 latency measured and documented. Deliverable: public repo with README architecture diagram and a one-page design note on consistency choices. Hours: ~40 across weeks 3-6.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- On "3-10 years production backend": "My production experience is earlier in its arc than the top of your range, but I've built and operated streaming data systems end-to-end in school and research settings, and I've spent the last month going deep on exactly the stack in this job description. I'd rather show you that work than inflate a number."
- On finance: "I haven't worked in markets before. I learned the basics of rates, FX, and derivatives because this role needs them, and I built a small pricing notebook to make sure I actually understood the math — what I'd need from the team is the domain depth that only comes from sitting next to your quants."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: The Twitch SDE II Fintech role is fundamentally an SAP + AWS + agentic-AI job, and her profile covers the AWS/Python/AI side well but has zero SAP (ABAP, CDS, RAP, OData), which the JD demands at 4+ years — a structural gap no study plan can close. The plan focuses on the learnable layer (OAuth 2.0/OIDC, API contract testing, AWS CDK, Step Functions/DynamoDB, MCP servers and Bedrock agents, finance-domain vocabulary) and on one honest interview story for the SAP gap.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python | Have | "Proficiency in at least one modern language beyond ABAP — Python, TypeScript/JavaScript" |
| AWS Lambda, S3, EC2 | Have | "Build and operate AWS-native services (Lambda, Step Functions, API Gateway, S3...)" |
| CI/CD, Git, Docker | Have | "Deploy... including CI/CD pipelines, IAM roles" |
| Design patterns / SOLID | Have | "Strong understanding of object-oriented design patterns (Factory, Strategy, Observer, Template Method)" |
| REST APIs (Flask) | Have | "API-Based (REST, OData, SOAP) patterns" |
| LangChain, prompt engineering, LLM workflows | Have | "Demonstrated heavy use of AI tools... integrated into your daily engineering workflow" |
| ABAP, CDS views, AMDP, HANA SQL, RAP, OData/SEGW, BAPI/RFC, S/4HANA, BTP, Fiori | Missing — structural | Core of the role: "4+ years of hands-on SAP development experience" |
| Finance domain (FI/CO, AP, AR, GL) | Missing — learnable | "Finance domain knowledge — familiarity with FI/CO, FI/CA, AP, AR or GL" |
| OAuth 2.0 / OIDC | Missing — learnable | "Understanding of OAuth 2.0 authorization flows... and OpenID Connect" |
| Postman/Bruno API testing | Missing — learnable | "Testing and debugging APIs using tools like Bruno or Postman" |
| AWS CDK (TypeScript/Python), multi-env topology | Missing — learnable | "Deploy and manage the AWS infrastructure... using CDK" |
| Step Functions, DynamoDB, API Gateway, ECS/Fargate | Missing — learnable | Named AWS services she hasn't run in production |
| MCP servers, Bedrock agents, Claude workflows | Missing — learnable (extends her LangChain base) | "MCP servers, Bedrock-based agents, and Claude-powered workflows" |
| Redshift | Never-claim | "Data pipelines that move financial data between SAP, Redshift, and enterprise applications" |
| Terraform | Never-claim | JD accepts "CDK, Terraform, or CloudFormation" — learn CDK, never claim Terraform |
| Stakeholder collaboration with Finance/Accounting/Tax | Missing — learnable (soft) | "Collaborate with Finance, Accounting, and Tax stakeholders" |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **SAP vocabulary, honestly framed.** Learn what ABAP, CDS views, RAP, OData, and S/4HANA actually are so she can discuss the role's SAP half intelligently without implying experience. Resource: openSAP's free "Modernization with SAP S/4HANA" / SAP Learning ABAP overview courses. Self-check: in 30 minutes, explain out loud what a CDS view and a RAP business object are, and where OData sits between SAP and AWS middleware.
2. **OAuth 2.0 and OIDC.** JD: "authorization code, client credentials." Resource: OAuth 2.0 Simplified (oauth.net) by Aaron Parecki. Self-check: whiteboard both flows, name where tokens live, and explain why client credentials fits SAP-to-AWS machine integrations.
3. **API contract testing with Postman or Bruno.** Resource: Postman Learning Center (free). Self-check: build a small collection against a public API with auth, environment variables, and response-assertion tests in 30 minutes.
4. **Finance vocabulary (AP, AR, GL, reconciliation, variance).** Resource: free "Financial Accounting" fundamentals on Coursera audit track or Corporate Finance Institute's free accounting guides. Self-check: define GL posting, three-way match, and month-end reconciliation, and tie each to an automation opportunity.
5. **AWS Step Functions + DynamoDB + API Gateway basics.** Resource: AWS free workshops (Step Functions workshop, serverless-workshops). Self-check: describe a state machine that calls a (mock) SAP OData endpoint, retries, and writes to DynamoDB.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **AWS CDK in Python.** JD wants IaC "in a team setting"; Terraform is never-claim, so CDK is the compliant path. Artefact: a public GitHub repo deploying a Lambda + API Gateway + DynamoDB stack with beta/gamma/prod stages and a CI/CD pipeline (she has CI/CD), README explaining IAM roles and VPC choices.
2. **MCP server from scratch.** JD: "MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers." Artefact: a small MCP server (Python) exposing finance-reconciliation tools to a Claude client, with a written walkthrough of the protocol's tools/resources model.
3. **Bedrock agents / agentic workflow.** She has LangChain — port the mental model. Artefact: a notebook + repo where a Bedrock (or local-LLM fallback, she runs Ollama) agent automates a variance-analysis task over CSV ledgers, with tool-calling traces shown.
4. **Data pipeline design: SAP → Redshift shape, without claiming Redshift.** Learn Redshift concepts (distribution keys, COPY, Spectrum) to discuss the JD's pipeline requirement conceptually only. Artefact: a written architecture walkthrough (markdown, diagrams) of moving financial extracts from an OData endpoint through S3 into a columnar warehouse, explicitly framed as a design study.
5. **Stakeholder translation practice.** JD: "translate business requirements into technical solutions." Artefact: a one-page requirements-to-design memo for the reconciliation use case, written as if for a Finance stakeholder — doubles as interview prep material.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

**"SAP-meets-AWS" agentic finance integration — not built yet.** None of her projects is an ERP-to-cloud integration or a production-style agentic automation; the JD centers exactly that.
- Goal: simulate the role's core pattern end-to-end at hobby scale.
- Data: synthetic general-ledger/AP records (extend her Expense Tracker dataset with vendor invoices and PO numbers).
- Stack: Flask mock "SAP" OData API (she has Flask) → AWS Lambda + Step Functions + DynamoDB + S3, all deployed via CDK (Python) with CI/CD; MCP server exposing reconciliation tools to a Claude/Bedrock agent.
- Agent task: automated three-way-match reconciliation and variance flagging with a human-readable report.
- Evaluation: match rate on 200 seeded transactions, with injected mismatches caught; OAuth 2.0 client-credentials auth on the mock API.
- Deliverable: public repo, architecture diagram, 10-minute demo video, design memo.
- Hours: ~40-50 over weeks 2-5. Covers Tier 2 items 1-3 and 5 in one build.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **SAP (4+ years ABAP/CDS/RAP/OData):** "I want to be upfront: I haven't worked inside SAP — my background is Python and AWS data and ML systems. I've been studying how CDS views, RAP, and OData fit together so I understand what I'd be building against, and my AWS and API experience maps directly onto the cloud half of this role, but the SAP-side depth would be a genuine ramp for me."
- **Finance domain:** "I'm not an accountant, but I've learned the AP/AR/GL vocabulary and built a reconciliation automation prototype, so I understand the workflows Finance teams care about and I know the questions to ask them."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is actually learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: ZoomInfo's Software Engineer III - Data Acquisition role is a strong match on her existing Java, Airflow, Kafka, Spark, Flink, ETL and SQL base; the real prep work is GCP-specific services (Pub/Sub, Dataflow/Beam, DataProc, GCS) and data-acquisition engineering depth, plus honest framing of the 3+ years production-experience gap. Kubernetes, Terraform, Snowflake and BigQuery appear in the JD's nice-to-haves but are on her never-claim list: she may learn them here, never assert them.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Java, OOP ("Strong proficiency with Java") | Have | Core language of the acquisition services |
| Apache Airflow ("workflow orchestration") | Have | Scheduled batch ETL/ELT jobs |
| Apache Kafka ("streaming technologies such as Kafka") | Have | Event-driven ingestion |
| Apache Spark / PySpark ("DataProc, Spark") | Have | Distributed processing |
| ETL/ELT, data validation and quality ("ingest, validate, normalize, enrich") | Have | Core of Data Acquisition |
| SQL, schema design, data modeling | Have | Storage/query and data quality work |
| Cloud, AWS ("at least one cloud provider") | Have | Cloud-fluent, but JD prefers GCP |
| Docker, CI/CD, Grafana, Linux | Have | Production engineering practices, observability |
| GCP services: GCS, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, DataProc ("preferably GCP") | Missing, learnable | Their actual stack; AWS concepts transfer |
| Apache Beam / Google Dataflow | Missing, learnable | Named first in their processing list |
| Pipeline observability at scale ("throughput, latency, cost, error rates") | Missing, learnable | They probe operational maturity |
| Controlled backfills, dedup strategies | Missing, learnable | Data-quality interview staples |
| 3+ years professional engineering, "operating production data pipelines" | Missing, structural | Time and production scale cannot be compressed into weeks |
| Kubernetes/GKE, Terraform, Snowflake, BigQuery, Spark Streaming (nice-to-haves) | Never-claim | May be studied privately; never asserted as hers |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **GCP vocabulary via AWS mapping.** Learn GCS, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, DataProc as counterparts to S3, Kafka, Glue/EMR. Resource: Google Cloud's free "GCP for AWS Professionals" docs and free tier. Self-check: in 30 min, explain aloud when ZoomInfo would pick Pub/Sub vs Kafka and Dataflow vs DataProc, with one trade-off each.
2. **Apache Beam programming model.** PCollections, ParDo, windowing, watermarks, triggers. Resource: Beam Programming Guide (beam.apache.org). Self-check: draw a session-windowed pipeline on paper and explain what a watermark does to late data.
3. **Data acquisition domain language.** Ingestion, normalization, deduplication, enrichment, backfill, schema validation — the JD's own verbs. Resource: Fundamentals of Data Engineering (Reis & Housley), free chapters via O'Reilly trial. Self-check: whiteboard an end-to-end acquisition pipeline in 30 min and name the failure mode at each stage.
4. **Beam-vs-Spark/Flink positioning.** They list Beam, Spark and Flink alternatives; interviewers test judgment. Resource: Beam capability matrix + Dataflow docs. Self-check: 30-min written comparison of Beam vs Spark for a near-real-time feed.
5. **Honest positioning script.** Prepare a 60-second answer on where she is with GCP: strong AWS/Kafka/Spark base, actively ramping on GCP. Self-check: record it, replay, remove anything that overstates.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Beam/Dataflow batch pipeline.** Build a Java Beam job that ingests a public dataset, validates schema, dedups and writes partitioned output, run locally on DirectRunner. Artefact: GitHub repo with README, sample input/output and design notes.
2. **Streaming ingestion demo.** Pub/Sub (free tier) or local emulator feeding a Beam streaming job with windowing and late-data handling. Artefact: same repo, second module, plus a 1-page walkthrough of throughput and watermark behavior.
3. **Pipeline observability lab.** Instrument the pipeline with throughput, latency and error-rate metrics into Grafana (already Have). Artefact: dashboard screenshot plus a written SLI/SLO definition for the pipeline.
4. **Data-quality and backfill design doc.** Write how she would do schema validation, dedup, retries and a controlled backfill for a 1TB/day feed. Artefact: 2-page design document in the repo.
5. **Failure-mode drill.** Practice troubleshooting narratives: skewed keys, poison messages, slow sinks, cost spikes on Dataflow. Artefact: written incident walkthrough (symptom, hypothesis, fix, prevention) for two simulated failures.

## Build-now project (not built yet)

She has streaming/ML projects but no data-acquisition pipeline project; this JD needs one.

- Goal: mini B2B-style data acquisition system mirroring the JD's "acquire, transform, validate, store".
- Data: public company/domain datasets (e.g., SEC EDGAR filings or open business registries), plus a simulated webhook feed.
- Stack: Java + Apache Beam (batch + streaming), Pub/Sub emulator or Kafka, Airflow for scheduling, PostgreSQL sink, Docker Compose.
- Evaluation: dedup rate, schema-rejection rate, end-to-end latency, restart/backfill correctness after a kill.
- Deliverable: public repo with architecture diagram, Grafana dashboard, and a README covering failure modes.
- Hours: ~40 over weeks 2-5, overlapping Tier 2 items 1-3.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- "I have under three years of professional experience, so I won't claim otherwise; what I bring is hands-on pipeline work with Airflow, Kafka, Spark and Flink in research and project settings, and I'd rather show you my beam acquisition repo than inflate a number."
- "My production exposure is on AWS, not GCP, and not yet at ZoomInfo's scale. The concepts — partitioning, backpressure, exactly-once trade-offs — transfer, and I've been drilling the GCP equivalents specifically for this role."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before, and never any never-claim skill in any wording.
