plan.summary: Chime's AI/ML Engineer role is heavily aligned with her registered stack (Python, SQL, PyTorch, Spark/PySpark, Airflow, Kafka, AWS core), so the plan concentrates on production-ML judgment topics the JD stresses: leakage, imbalance, train/serve skew, monitoring and retraining, plus Snowflake/SageMaker/Redis concepts she may learn but must never claim. The structural gaps are years of production deep-learning experience at scale and a publication record (Foundation Models team), for which honest interview answers are provided.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python, SQL | Have | "Strong proficiency in Python and SQL" |
| PyTorch, deep learning | Have | "deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch" |
| Spark / PySpark | Have | "distributed compute such as Spark or PySpark" |
| Airflow, Kafka | Have | named under "modern ML infrastructure" |
| AWS (EC2, S3, Lambda, Glue, EMR) | Have | "AWS and tools such as…" |
| Docker, CI/CD, Flask | Have | supports "deployment… and an MLOps mindset" |
| Leakage, class imbalance, train/serve skew, label definition | Learnable (this plan) | "Comfort with messy real-world data, including label definition, leakage, class imbalance, and train/serve skew" |
| Monitoring, retraining, drift | Learnable (this plan) | "deployment, monitoring, and retraining" |
| Evaluation design / metric selection | Learnable (this plan) | "knowing which metric actually answers the question" |
| Experimentation / A/B testing | Learnable (this plan) | "use experimentation to prove impact" |
| Fraud/credit domain basics, explainability & fairness | Learnable (this plan) | Trust & Safety and Lending nice-to-haves |
| Snowflake | Never-claim (learn only) | named in JD infrastructure list |
| SageMaker | Never-claim (learn only) | named in JD infrastructure list |
| Redis | Never-claim (learn only) | named in JD infrastructure list |
| Years of production DL at millions-of-users scale | Structural | "Experience building and deploying deep learning models in production" |
| Publication record (Foundation Models) | Structural | "applied research with a publication record" |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Train/serve skew and leakage vocabulary.** Learn the canonical failure modes and how features pipelines prevent them. Resource: Google ML Crash Course, "Production ML Systems" section. Self-check: explain, in 5 minutes, three ways leakage enters a fraud model and how you'd detect each.
2. **Class imbalance and metric choice.** Precision/recall tradeoffs, PR-AUC vs ROC-AUC, thresholding. Resource: scikit-learn imbalanced-learn user guide. Self-check: given 0.1% fraud rate, argue in writing why accuracy is useless and pick a metric.
3. **Monitoring and retraining fundamentals.** Data drift, concept drift, retraining triggers. Resource: Evidently AI docs (open-source drift monitoring). Self-check: sketch a monitoring dashboard for a deployed model — 5 metrics, one alert rule each.
4. **Experimentation basics.** A/B test design, novelty effects, guardrail metrics. Resource: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (chapter summaries via exp-platform.com notes). Self-check: design an A/B test for a new credit-limit model in 10 bullet points.
5. **Snowflake/SageMaker/Redis concepts — learn, never claim.** Read Snowflake's architecture overview, SageMaker's pipeline concepts, and Redis's caching role in real-time inference, so you can discuss them as "I've studied these; my hands-on work is on AWS core, Airflow, and Kafka." Self-check: explain where each sits in Chime's stack in one sentence.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Feature pipeline with leakage-safe design.** Build a batch feature pipeline in PySpark with point-in-time joins. Artefact: GitHub repo with a README walkthrough of one leakage bug you deliberately created and caught.
2. **End-to-end model monitoring demo.** Train a classifier, simulate drift, detect it. Artefact: Jupyter notebook with Evidently reports before/after drift, plus a written retraining policy.
3. **Class imbalance on a fraud-like dataset.** IEEE-CIS fraud data; compare PR-AUC across sampling strategies. Artefact: notebook with a metric-selection argument written for a non-technical PM.
4. **Real-time inference path.** Extend her Kafka/Flink experience into model serving: Flink SQL feature computation feeding a PyTorch model. Artefact: small repo, docker-compose, latency numbers documented.
5. **Lending explainability & fairness.** SHAP on a credit dataset, plus a fairness check (demographic parity gap). Artefact: written walkthrough titled "How I'd explain and audit a credit model" — directly answers the Lending nice-to-have.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has no end-to-end *production-style* ML project with monitoring and retraining; the JD demands exactly that. **Fraud detection system, "not built yet":** Goal — end-to-end fraud classifier on IEEE-CIS data, framed like Chime Trust & Safety. Data — IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection (Kaggle). Stack — PyTorch + scikit-learn models, PySpark feature pipeline, Flask serving, Kafka for event stream, Airflow for scheduled retraining, Docker, Evidently for drift monitoring. Evaluation — PR-AUC at fixed false-positive rate, documented leakage audit, drift-detection demo. Deliverable — public repo with architecture diagram, README, and a 2-page writeup connecting model metrics to business outcomes (false-decline cost vs fraud loss). Hours — ~40 over weeks 2-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- Production DL at scale: "I've built and deployed deep learning models in research and personal projects, and I've studied how production ML systems fail and recover. I haven't yet owned a model serving millions of users — that's exactly what I want to learn here, and I've spent the last month building a monitored, retraining-capable system to close that gap deliberately."
- Publication record: "I don't have publications; my research work in the AICV lab was applied. I'm strongest on the applied engineering side, so Trust & Safety or Lending is likely a better match than Foundation Models."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: Reddit's Ingestion Platform role centers on Kafka-to-warehouse data movement, connector APIs, and pipeline reliability — much of which she already has (Kafka, Flink, Spark, Airflow, Python). The plan focuses on what she lacks: Apache Iceberg, GCP/GCS vocabulary, ingestion-platform architecture patterns (control/data plane, DLQs, schema evolution), plus honest scripts for the structural gaps (2+ years production experience, large-scale system design evidence), with Kubernetes and BigQuery strictly learn-only since they are on her never-claim list.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Apache Kafka | Have | Core source system: "100B events per day" ingested |
| Apache Flink / Spark | Have | "batch and streaming based ML and BI workloads" |
| Airflow, Python, Java | Have | "orchestrate these data workloads"; OOP proficiency |
| Amazon S3, Docker, CI/CD, Grafana | Have | "paths to S3/GCS", deployment safety, "actionable observability and alerting" |
| Delta Lake | Have | Adjacent to Iceberg; transferable table-format knowledge |
| Apache Iceberg | Missing, learnable | "production-ready paths to S3/GCS and Apache Iceberg" |
| GCP / GCS | Missing, learnable | "Kafka-to-BigQuery", "paths to S3/GCS" (she knows AWS only) |
| Control plane vs data plane, connector/target-manager APIs | Missing, learnable | "pipeline APIs, controllers, connectors, target managers, sink integrations" |
| Deduplication, dead-letter queues, schema evolution | Missing, learnable | Named verbatim as "reusable capabilities" and reliability practices |
| Platform migration strategy | Missing, learnable | "safe, incremental, and low-touch" migrations off legacy systems |
| Kubernetes | Never-claim — learn only | "pipelines running across Kubernetes clusters"; do not claim it |
| BigQuery | Never-claim — learn only | The current Kafka sink; learn vocabulary, never claim experience |
| Go / Scala | Never-claim | Listed under "Python, Scala, Go, or Java" — Python/Java already cover this |
| 2+ years production SWE experience | Structural | Hard requirement; cannot be learned in weeks |
| Demonstrated large-scale production system design | Structural | "Demonstrated expertise in designing and implementing large-scale systems" |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Ingestion-platform vocabulary: control plane vs data plane.** Learn how controllers, connectors, and sink integrations divide responsibilities. Resource: Confluent's free "Inside Kafka Connect" / data pipeline architecture articles. Self-check: in 30 min, whiteboard a Kafka-to-warehouse platform and label which components are control plane vs data plane, out loud, no notes.
2. **Apache Iceberg fundamentals.** Contrast with Delta Lake (which she has): table format, snapshots, hidden partitioning. Resource: Tabular's free "Apache Iceberg — Getting Started" guide. Self-check: explain schema evolution and partition evolution in Iceberg vs Delta Lake in 5 minutes each.
3. **Delivery semantics: exactly-once, deduplication, dead-letter queues.** The JD lists these as platform capabilities. Resource: Confluent Developer free course module on error handling and DLQs. Self-check: describe three ways duplicates enter a Kafka pipeline and one mitigation per way.
4. **GCP vocabulary for an AWS person.** GCS vs S3, BigQuery slots vs Redshift-style warehouses (learn-only; BigQuery is never-claim). Resource: Google Cloud's free doc "Google Cloud for AWS professionals". Self-check: map ten AWS services she uses to their GCP equivalents from memory.
5. **Schema evolution and registry patterns.** The JD names "schemas" and "schema evolution" under reliability. Resource: Confluent Schema Registry fundamentals (free docs). Self-check: explain backward vs forward compatibility and what breaks a consumer in each.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Iceberg depth: compaction, snapshot expiration, partition evolution.** Artefact: a Jupyter notebook using PySpark (Have) writing Iceberg tables, demonstrating a schema change and a partition-spec change with before/after query results.
2. **End-to-end ingestion pipeline with DLQ and dedup.** Build Kafka → Flink → Iceberg with a poison-record path. Artefact: a public repo with README, docker-compose, and a test that injects a malformed event and shows it land in the DLQ.
3. **Kubernetes for data workloads (learn-only, never claim).** Resource: the free official Kubernetes tutorials plus minikube. Artefact: a written walkthrough of deploying the pipeline's components on minikube — kept as a private learning note, since Kubernetes is on her never-claim list.
4. **Sink design: BigQuery-style warehouse vs Iceberg-on-object-storage.** Learn-only for BigQuery. Artefact: a one-page written comparison of cost, latency, and schema-evolution trade-offs between a managed warehouse sink and an open table format — exactly the "beyond Kafka-to-BigQuery" expansion the JD describes.
5. **Pipeline observability.** She has Grafana; extend it to ingestion metrics (lag, DLQ rate, throughput). Artefact: a Grafana dashboard JSON plus alert rules committed to the repo from item 2.

## Build-now project (not built yet)

- Goal: a miniature self-serve ingestion platform, mirroring the JD's control plane/data plane split.
- Data: synthetic clickstream events (~1M/day via a Python generator), 5% deliberately malformed.
- Stack: Kafka (source), Flink SQL (transform + dedup), Iceberg on MinIO as the S3-compatible sink, Airflow for orchestration, Grafana for lag/DLQ dashboards, GitHub Actions for CI/CD.
- Control plane: a small Flask (Have) API that registers a new "pipeline" and writes its config; a controller loop that applies it.
- Reliability features: dead-letter topic for malformed events, schema evolution demo (add a field mid-stream), idempotent sink writes.
- Evaluation: inject a schema change and a poison record; pipeline must keep running, DLQ must capture the record, new field must appear queryable.
- Deliverable: public repo with architecture diagram, README, demo script, and a 10-minute recorded walkthrough.
- Hours: ~60-75 over weeks 2-5. Kubernetes deployment optional and kept out of all public claims.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **2+ years production experience:** "My production experience comes from research and project environments rather than two years in industry. What I can show is that I build like it's production — tested, monitored, documented — and I'm upfront that I'm earlier in that journey than the posting describes."
- **Demonstrated large-scale system design:** "I haven't operated systems at Reddit's 100B-events-per-day scale. I have built streaming pipelines end to end and studied how systems like this one are architected, and I'd want to earn that scale experience here rather than pretend I already have it."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill above is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before, and never-claim items never.

| AWS (EC2, S3, Lambda, Glue) | Have | "Developing software in AWS or similar cloud-computing services" |
| Computer vision, content understanding | Have | "experimenting with new techniques in LLM, computer vision, inference and model evaluation" |
| LLM model evaluation | Missing, learnable (3-6 wks) | "Experience with LLM model evaluations" — a hard requirement |
| LLM inference | Missing, learnable | Bonus: "Experience with computer vision, LLM inference, content understanding" |
| Statistics / experimentation | Missing, learnable | Implied by "model evaluation" and GTM Science's ads work |
| GTM domain: Ads, Brand Safety, Creator Sponsorship | Missing, learnable (vocabulary) | "ambiguous business problems across… Ads, Brand Safety, Creator Sponsorship" |
| Stakeholder communication | Missing, learnable | "working with both technical and non-technical partners and stakeholders" |
| 3+ years industry applied ML (Master's track) | Missing, structural | "3+ years of applied ML experience (Master's)" |
| Owning projects with numerous scientists/engineers | Missing, structural | "Experience owning projects that involve numerous scientists and engineers" |
| PhD specialization | Structural, bonus only | "Bonus Points: PhD" — her MS already satisfies the degree line |

No JD requirement touches her never-claim list (no SageMaker, MLflow, Kubeflow, dbt, etc. named).

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **LLM evaluation fundamentals** — the JD's "Experience with LLM model evaluations." Learn: task metrics (accuracy, F1, ROUGE, BERTScore), LLM-as-judge, human eval, golden datasets. Resource: Hugging Face Cookbook evaluation guide (huggingface.co/learn/cookbook, free). Self-check (30 min): explain in writing how she'd evaluate a stream-title classifier three ways, and when each fails.
2. **Statistics refresh: hypothesis testing & A/B tests** — the "statistics" gap. Learn: p-values, confidence intervals, power, novelty effects. Resource: StatQuest's "Statistics Fundamentals" playlist (free, YouTube). Self-check: design an A/B test for a new ad format on paper in 30 minutes, including sample-size reasoning.
3. **GTM vocabulary** — "Ads, Brand Safety, Creator Sponsorship and Content Understanding." Learn: CPM/CPC, viewability, brand-safety tiers, sponsorship measurement. Resource: Twitch Advertising's public product pages and the Twitch Blog (free). Self-check: explain to a friend in 30 minutes how Twitch makes money and where ML enters each revenue line.
4. **Stakeholder communication** — the "stakeholders" gap. Learn: framing results for non-technical partners (decision-first memos, uncertainty statements). Resource: Google's People + AI Guidebook, chapter on communicating ML (free). Self-check: write a one-page project brief for a brand-safety model, jargon-free, in 30 minutes.
5. **Twitch product fluency** — bonus: "Familiarity with Twitch, its business, and its community." Resource: Twitch Creator Camp + 3 recent engineering blog posts (free). Self-check: name five content-signal problems Twitch likely has, from the product itself, in 30 minutes.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Build an LLM eval harness.** Learn promptfoo's config, assertions, and model-graded evals (promptfoo.dev docs, free). Artefact: a public repo evaluating three prompt variants for a "brand-safe vs unsafe stream title" classifier, with a results table and a written failure analysis.
2. **Classical vs SOTA judgment** — "Know when to use a classical ML model versus a state-of-the-art one." Train logistic regression, then fine-tune a small transformer on the same text-classification set. Artefact: notebook comparing accuracy, latency, cost per 1k inferences, with a one-paragraph decision memo.
3. **LLM inference basics** — bonus "LLM inference." Learn batching, quantization, KV-cache, token-cost math via her existing Ollama/Llama 3.2 setup. Artefact: a benchmark notebook measuring latency/throughput at 3 quantization levels, with a cost extrapolation to Twitch-scale volumes.
4. **Experimentation depth.** Learn CUPED, multiple comparisons, guardrail metrics. Resource: "Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments" summary notes + Khan Academy stats (free). Artefact: notebook simulating an A/A and A/B test on synthetic ad-click data, showing false-positive control.
5. **Multimodal content understanding.** Combine her CV strengths (YOLO, Res-UNet) with text: classify clips using thumbnail + title + transcript embeddings (FAISS, nomic-embed-text). Artefact: Streamlit demo repo classifying Twitch-category thumbnails with an embedding-similarity explainer.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

**Status: not built yet.** The JD wants "prototype and put them into production" applied to content signals — she has no LLM-evaluation/content-understanding project.
- Goal: brand-safety scoring service for live-stream metadata.
- Data: public Twitch category/thumbnail samples + self-written titles labeled by rubric.
- Stack: Python, PyTorch, Ollama (Llama 3.2), FAISS, Flask, promptfoo.
- Evaluation: golden set of 200 labeled titles; precision/recall per brand-safety tier; LLM-as-judge agreement score.
- Deliverable: repo with eval harness, API endpoint, README decision memo (classical vs LLM trade-offs).
- Hours: ~25 across weeks 3-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **Years of industry applied ML:** "My applied ML work has been in research labs and personal production-style projects — gait assessment and virtual try-on in the AICV Lab — not three years in industry. What I can show is end-to-end ownership: data, modeling, evaluation, and deployment on each."
- **Owning multi-scientist projects:** "I haven't yet led a project staffed by multiple scientists. I have owned projects solo end-to-end and collaborated across hardware and software teams, and I'd be transparent that team-scale science leadership is the growth I want from this role."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: For Block's Reconciliation & Reporting role, her registered skills already cover the entire technical stack the JD requires (Python/Java, SQL, Airflow, Spark, Kafka, AWS, CI/CD); the real preparation targets are payments-domain knowledge (settlement, card-network files, ISO-8583), double-entry bookkeeping and reconciliation concepts, and tax/regulatory vocabulary (1099, CESOP, AML/KYC). The structural gaps are the 3+ years of professional experience and production payments-domain experience, both answerable honestly, and a small self-built reconciliation pipeline project would give her a concrete proof artefact for the technical round.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python, Java, SQL | Have | "Proficiency in at least one major programming language (e.g., Java, Python, Go) and solid SQL" |
| Airflow, Spark/PySpark, Kafka, ETL | Have | "batch- or event-driven data pipelines... workflow-orchestration (e.g., Airflow, Temporal, Spark)" |
| Delta Lake, AWS, CI/CD, testing, observability | Have | "cloud data warehouses... Delta Lake, Kafka"; "CI/CD, and observability" |
| Bachelor's degree | Have | JD requires a technical degree or equivalent; she holds degrees |
| Payments lifecycle: authorization, clearing, settlement, ISO-8583, card-network file formats | Missing, learnable | "Familiarity with the payments ecosystem... card-network settlement file formats, or ISO-8583" |
| Double-entry bookkeeping, reconciliation concepts | Missing, learnable | "Understanding of accounting principles, double-entry bookkeeping, and financial reconciliation processes" |
| Tax/regulatory reporting vocabulary: 1099 family, CESOP, AML/KYC, TIN validation | Missing, learnable | "US IRS information returns (the 1099 family...) and international regimes such as EU-wide CESOP" |
| Temporal | Missing, learnable | Listed beside Airflow, which she has; concepts transfer |
| 3+ years professional experience | Structural | "3+ years of professional software or data engineering experience" |
| Production payments/financial-systems experience | Structural | "Exposure to financial, tax, regulatory, or payments reporting" (nice-to-have, but probed) |
| Snowflake, BigQuery, Hadoop | Never-claim | Nice-to-have list; on her never-claim list — may be learned later, never asserted now |
| Kubernetes, Terraform | Never-claim | "Exposure to cloud platforms (AWS, Kubernetes) and infrastructure-as-code (Terraform)" — never-claim list |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Payments lifecycle vocabulary** — Learn the money path the JD describes: merchant, acquirer, card network, issuer; authorization vs. clearing vs. settlement. Resource: Stripe's free "Payment lifecycle" and card-payments documentation. Self-check (30 min): on one blank page, draw and narrate the path of a $50 card payment from tap to merchant payout, naming each party and file handoff.
2. **Card-network settlement files and ISO-8583 basics** — Learn what a Visa/Mastercard settlement/report file contains (record types, amounts, fees, reconciliation totals) and what ISO-8583 messages look like (MTI, data elements). Resource: the open-source jPOS documentation and its ISO-8583 tutorial. Self-check: explain fields 2, 4, and 39 and why a settlement file's control totals matter.
3. **Double-entry bookkeeping and reconciliation** — Learn debits/credits, journals, ledgers, and what "reconciling two data sources" means operationally (matching, exceptions, breaks, aging). Resource: AccountingCoach's free double-entry and bank-reconciliation modules. Self-check: write the journal entries for a merchant sale minus processing fee, then define three ways two ledgers can disagree.
4. **Regulatory reporting vocabulary** — Learn what a 1099-K is, who receives it and why, what CESOP requires of payment processors in the EU, and where AML/KYC and TIN validation fit. Resource: IRS.gov pages on Form 1099-K and TIN matching; the EU Commission's CESOP overview. Self-check: in five sentences each, explain 1099-K and CESOP to a hypothetical finance partner.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Reconciliation matching engine design** — Go deep on matching algorithms: one-to-one, many-to-one, tolerance windows, exception queues. Artefact: a notebook reconciling two synthetic CSV "ledgers" (internal transactions vs. a mock network settlement file), producing a breaks report with aging. Public repo, README explaining design choices.
2. **Exactly-once semantics and idempotency in pipelines** — The JD stresses "accurate, reliable, timely" at payments scale; learn idempotent writes, dedup keys, replay strategies in Kafka/Spark (she has both; this is depth, not breadth). Artefact: a short written walkthrough in the repo showing how the pipeline survives a double-delivered file without double-counting money.
3. **Temporal vs. Airflow mental model** — JD names Temporal; she knows Airflow. Resource: Temporal's official docs and free "Temporal 101" course. Artefact: a one-page comparison doc plus a tiny Temporal workflow (hello-reconciliation) in the repo.
4. **Observability and auditability for financial data** — Learn lineage, data-quality checks, and what "end-to-end traceability of money" demands (immutable logs, reconciliation dashboards). Artefact: extend the project with a small Grafana/streamlit-style metrics page or markdown dashboard showing match rates, exception counts, and pipeline run history.
5. **AI-assisted development judgment** — The JD explicitly asks for "Proficiency in using AI tools... with the judgment to recognize where output needs additional validation." Artefact: a short repo note documenting where AI was used in the project and how each suggestion was validated (tests, review, experiments).

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

**Not built yet.** Mini reconciliation and reporting pipeline (she has no reconciliation/financial-reporting project type).
- Goal: reconcile mock card-network settlement files against internal transaction records and emit standardized journals.
- Data: self-generated synthetic CSVs — internal payments table plus a Visa-style settlement file with deliberate mismatches (missing, duplicated, amount-drifted rows).
- Stack: Python, PostgreSQL, Airflow for orchestration, PySpark optional for scale demo; plain CI via GitHub Actions.
- Evaluation: match rate, exception count, break aging; journals must tie to control totals to the cent.
- Deliverable: public repo with README, architecture diagram, tests, sample outputs, and a 5-minute walkthrough write-up.
- Hours: ~35-45 over weeks 2-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- On experience: "I meet the technical bar through my project and research work, and I'm upfront that my professional tenure is shorter than three years — I've compensated by owning pipelines end-to-end, from design to operation, and I'd bring that same ownership here."
- On payments domain: "I haven't worked in payments production systems yet. I've studied the settlement lifecycle and reconciliation mechanics specifically for this team, and I learn domain context fast — my data-engineering fundamentals transfer directly."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill above is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: Palantir's Backend Infrastructure role targets distributed systems, search/indexing, and container orchestration at scale; she already covers Java, Spark, Kafka, Flink, Docker and AWS, so the plan focuses on Cassandra, Gradle, observability, and distributed-systems fundamentals. Kubernetes, Go, Rust and Elasticsearch appear in the JD but sit on her never-claim list — they are learning targets for interview fluency only, never skills to assert, and the structural gaps (production HA systems experience, security clearance) get honest scripted answers.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Java | Have | "Strong coding skills... such as Java, C++, Python, Rust" |
| Python, C++ | Have | Same requirement line; Palantir polyglot backends |
| Spark, Kafka, Flink | Have | "Open-source technologies like Cassandra, ElasticSearch, Spark, Kafka, Kubernetes, Flink" |
| Docker, Linux, AWS, Git, CI/CD, TDD, Multithreading, Design patterns | Have | "cloud infrastructure", "Industry-standard build tooling", "defensive" code quality bar |
| CS/engineering degree | Have | "Engineering background in Computer Science... or similar field" (MS, University of Arkansas) |
| Cassandra | Missing, learnable (this plan) | "Automating the deployment, management, and operations of... Cassandra, Elasticsearch, Kafka" |
| Gradle | Missing, learnable (this plan) | "Industry-standard build tooling, including Gradle and GitHub" |
| Distributed systems fundamentals | Missing, learnable (this plan) | "database technologies, distributed systems, large scale data systems" |
| Tracing / observability (OpenTelemetry) | Missing, learnable (this plan) | "Tracing and performance observability in high scale distributed microservice architectures" |
| Search & indexing internals | Missing, learnable (this plan) | "performant search and indexing ecosystem for complex granularly permissioned data" |
| Kubernetes | Never-claim (learn concepts only) | "scheduling hundreds of thousands of containers every hour" |
| Elasticsearch | Never-claim (learn concepts only) | Named in technologies and search responsibilities |
| Go, Rust | Never-claim (learn to read only) | "Different backend languages, including Java, Rust, and Go" |
| Production HA distributed systems experience | Missing, structural | "Experience developing and managing highly-available distributed systems is beneficial, but not required" |
| US security clearance | Structural (optional) | "beneficial, but not necessary" |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Distributed systems vocabulary.** JD: "distributed systems, large scale data systems." Learn: replication, partitioning, consistency models, CAP tradeoffs, leader election. Resource: MIT 6.824 lecture videos + notes (free, pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824). Self-check: in 30 min, whiteboard why a permissioned search system would pick quorum reads vs. leader reads, out loud.
2. **Cassandra data model.** JD: "Automating the deployment... of... Cassandra." Learn: partition keys, clustering columns, tunable consistency, why joins don't exist. Resource: official Apache Cassandra docs, "Cassandra Basics" (cassandra.apache.org/doc). Self-check: design a schema for time-series access logs in 30 min and defend the partition key.
3. **Container orchestration concepts (Kubernetes — learn, never claim).** JD: "orchestrating and efficiently scheduling hundreds of thousands of containers every hour." Learn: pods, schedulers, resource requests/limits, autoscaling. Resource: kubernetes.io tutorials (concepts sections only). Self-check: explain in 30 min what a scheduler does when a node fails mid-rollout.
4. **Search & indexing basics (Elasticsearch internals — concepts, never claim).** JD: "performant search and indexing ecosystem for complex granularly permissioned data." Learn: inverted indexes, Lucene segments, filter vs. query, how ACL filtering composes with ranking. Resource: Elasticsearch guide, "Elasticsearch from the Bottom Up" (free, elastic.co). Self-check: sketch query execution for a permission-filtered keyword search.
5. **Gradle + the honest-status story for every gap.** JD: "build tooling, including Gradle and GitHub." Learn: tasks, dependencies, build.gradle structure (she has Maven-adjacent instincts from Java). Resource: Gradle "Getting Started" guides (gradle.org/guides). Self-check: write a minimal Java build.gradle with a test task from memory, and rehearse one honest sentence per gap: "I haven't used X in production; here's what I know and how I'm learning it."

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Cassandra hands-on.** Run a 3-node local cluster, model real data, kill a node, observe hinted handoff. Artefact: a small repo with docker-compose cluster, schema, and a one-page benchmark writeup (throughput at ONE vs. QUORUM).
2. **Distributed tracing.** Instrument a two-service Java or Python demo with OpenTelemetry, export to Jaeger, break something on purpose, find it via traces. Artefact: repo plus a Grafana/Jaeger dashboard walkthrough doc (builds on her Grafana).
3. **Scheduler design literacy.** JD's "hundreds of thousands of containers every hour" is a Borg/Kubernetes-scale claim. Read the Google Borg paper and the Kubernetes scheduler docs. Artefact: a written two-page comparison, "how large-scale container schedulers make placement decisions," in her own words.
4. **Palantir stack reading fluency (Go/Rust — never claim).** Work through a short Go tutorial, enough to read infrastructure code in an interview pairing session without freezing. Artefact: annotated notes on one small open-source Go service (e.g., a Prometheus exporter), showing she can follow the code.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

Not triggered. The JD's project-shaped demands are CI/CD-adjacent automation (she has CI/CD) and distributed-infrastructure depth, which Tier 2 items 1-3 cover as artefacts. The tempting Kubernetes/Terraform build is off-limits as a claimable skill and must not become a resume line.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **Production distributed systems:** "I haven't operated highly-available distributed systems in production yet — my hands-on experience is project and research scale, with Kafka, Flink and Spark. I've spent the weeks since applying going deep on Cassandra internals and scheduler design, because that's the gap I knew this team would test."
- **Security clearance:** "I don't hold a clearance. The posting says it's beneficial but not necessary, and I'm fully willing to go through the process wherever I'm eligible."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — and Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Go and Rust stay off permanently, per her never-claim list.

limitations: The plan is built only from the job posting text; Palantir's actual interview loop for this team (question mix, pair-programming format, decomposition vs. coding emphasis) is not public and could shift priorities.

The never-claim list conflicts with the JD on Kubernetes, Elasticsearch, Go and Rust: these are treated as learn-for-fluency only, which limits how deep the plan can go on them without crossing the claim boundary.
Documentation URLs are cited from canonical locations but were not re-fetched and verified live during this analysis.

plan.summary: Lyft's Fulfillment MLE role is mostly covered on fundamentals (Python, PyTorch, an MS degree, streaming data skills), so the plan concentrates on the three genuine learnable gaps — statistics, deep-learning recommendation systems, and experiment design — plus honest framing for two structural gaps (production ML tenure and research-to-production experience). It sequences vocabulary for the screening call, depth work ending in proof artefacts for the technical round, and one not-yet-built recommender project.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| "Proficiency in Python" | Have | Production code for models |
| "TensorFlow, PyTorch, or similar" | Have (PyTorch registered) | Deep learning for recommenders |
| "BS/MS in Computer Science" | Have (MS, University of Arkansas) | Baseline credential |
| Kafka/Spark/Flink-style data pipelines | Have (registered) | Adjacent to "feature pipelines" |
| "statistical concepts such as hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and performance evaluation metrics" | Missing, learnable | Model evaluation vs KPIs |
| "deep learning technologies for recommendation systems" | Missing, learnable | Core Fulfillment matching work |
| "run experiments… against business KPIs" | Missing, learnable | A/B testing culture |
| "feature pipelines, model training workflows, and serving infrastructure" | Missing, learnable (conceptually) | Day-one architecture literacy |
| "translating state-of-the-art ML research into production systems" | Missing, structural | Needs production tenure |
| "2+ years of experience in machine learning" | Missing, structural | Cannot be compressed |
| "Golang" | Never-claim (on her list) | JD says "Python, Golang, **or** other" — Python satisfies it |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Statistics fundamentals** (JD: "hypothesis testing, regression analysis, performance evaluation metrics"). Learn: p-values, confidence intervals, Type I/II error, precision/recall/AUC, calibration. Resource: StatQuest video series (free, YouTube). Self-check: explain in 30 min, on paper, when precision beats recall for driver-rider matching, and what a p-value does *not* tell you.
2. **Recommender vocabulary** (JD: "deep learning technologies for recommendation systems"). Learn: candidate generation vs ranking, two-tower models, embeddings, negative sampling, NDCG/Recall@K. Resource: Google's free Recommendation Systems crash course (developers.google.com/machine-learning/recommendation). Self-check: whiteboard a two-tower architecture for matching riders to drivers in 30 min, including loss choice.
3. **A/B testing literacy** (JD: "run experiments, and drive continuous model improvement"). Learn: randomization, sample size, MDE, novelty effects, guardrail metrics. Resource: "Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments" summary chapters / exp-platform.com free notes. Self-check: design an experiment for a new matching model — hypothesis, primary metric, guardrails, runtime — in 30 min.
4. **Fulfillment domain fluency** (JD: "generate feasible offers… match rider requests with drivers… distributed state machine"). Learn: marketplace dynamics, ETA/pricing/matching interplay, batching vs instant matching. Resource: Lyft Engineering blog (eng.lyft.com), matching and marketplace posts. Self-check: explain in 30 min why matching is a bipartite optimization and where ML enters.
5. **Production ML lifecycle vocabulary** (JD: "feature pipelines, model training workflows, and serving infrastructure"). Learn: offline/online feature skew, training-serving consistency, model monitoring. Resource: "Designing Machine Learning Systems" (Chip Huyen) — early chapters via O'Reilly trial or library. Self-check: draw the lifecycle of one model from feature to retraining in 30 min.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Recommender depth in PyTorch.** Build a two-tower retrieval model on MovieLens-25M with embeddings, sampled softmax, and ANN retrieval via FAISS (already registered). Artefact: public repo with training notebook and a README comparing Recall@10 across two architectures.
2. **Real-time serving design.** Study latency budgets, feature stores, online inference, fallbacks. Artefact: a written design doc (2-3 pages) for serving the matching model under 100 ms, with a Flask prototype endpoint (Flask is registered).
3. **Lyft's actual stack.** Lyft open-sourced its ML workflow platform Flyte; read its docs and Lyft eng posts on Fulfillment. Artefact: a one-page architecture summary of how Lyft trains and serves matching models, with citations — usable verbatim in "why Lyft" answers.
4. **Evaluation against KPIs.** Connect offline metrics (AUC, NDCG) to online KPIs (conversion, wait time, cancellation). Artefact: a notebook simulating an A/B readout on synthetic data — power calculation, uplift estimate, guardrail check.
5. **Streaming-adjacent refresh for the state machine question.** She has Kafka/Flink; map them to "distributed state machine to track rides." Artefact: a short walkthrough comparing event-sourced ride-state tracking with her Medical IoT streaming project (PROJ-P01) patterns.

## Build-now project (not built yet)

She has no recommendation-system project, so one is required.

- **Goal:** end-to-end two-sided recommender mimicking rider-driver matching.
- **Data:** MovieLens-25M (public) as proxy for user-item matching; optional synthetic ETA feature.
- **Stack:** PyTorch (registered), FAISS (registered), Flask for serving (registered), Docker (registered). No never-claim tools.
- **Model:** two-tower retrieval + lightweight ranking layer; sampled softmax loss.
- **Evaluation:** Recall@K, NDCG@10 offline; latency benchmark of the Flask endpoint.
- **Deliverable:** public repo, training notebook, 1-page evaluation writeup, architecture diagram.
- **Hours:** ~40-50 over weeks 2-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **2+ years ML experience / research-to-production:** "My production experience so far is in data and streaming pipelines; my ML work is graduate research and project-based, which is why I built an end-to-end recommender before this call. I'm candid that this role would be my first production ML deployment, and I'd ramp with the team's platform rather than pretend otherwise."
- **Scale ("petabyte-scale data"):** "I've worked with streaming and distributed data systems, not petabyte-scale ML. I understand the patterns — partitioning, feature stores, online/offline skew — and I'd rather show you that understanding than claim scale I haven't run."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

sources.title: Lyft — Machine Learning Engineer, Fulfillment (job posting)
Google Machine Learning Crash Course — Recommendation Systems
Flyte — Lyft's open-sourced ML workflow platform

limitations: The genuine_gaps input contained raw JD sentence fragments rather than a clean skill list; only actual skill gaps were used.
Lyft's current internal stack details (beyond publicly documented Flyte and engineering-blog posts) are inferred from public sources and may be outdated.
Time estimates (3-6 weeks, 40-50 project hours) assume roughly 10-12 study hours per week alongside other applications.
No part of this plan modifies or implies resume content; structural-gap answers are interview framing only.

plan.summary: This plan targets Anthropic's Full Stack Engineer, Education Labs role: her Python/LLM/analytics base covers the back-of-stack demands, so prep concentrates on the front-of-frontend (TypeScript, React, motion polish), experimentation, and learning-science vocabulary. The real risks are structural — 6+ years of shipped web products and an interaction-design portfolio — so Tier 2 builds public proof artefacts to narrow that evidence gap honestly.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python, API design, data pipelines | Have | "Solid back-end and data pipeline experience: Python, API design, analytics infrastructure" — covered by Python, Flask, PostgreSQL, Airflow, Grafana |
| LLMs in production / AI-native UX | Have | "Building AI-native product experiences or working with LLMs in production" — LangChain, RAG, prompt engineering, Ollama |
| CSS | Have | "Strong front-end craft: ... CSS" — registered |
| CI/CD, Git, Docker | Have | Supports "independently driving features from prototype to production" |
| TypeScript/JavaScript | Missing, learnable | "Strong front-end craft: TypeScript/JavaScript" — transferable from Java/C#/Python |
| React | Missing, learnable; Never-claim | Core of their front-end stack; on never-claim list, so learn it, never assert it before re-registration |
| Interaction design, motion, "front-of-the-frontend" | Missing, learnable | "Particular attention to the front-of-the-frontend: motion, polish, and interaction feel" |
| Experimentation frameworks, A/B testing, capability analytics | Missing, learnable | "Analytics that measure capability development in production" |
| HCI / learning sciences fundamentals | Missing, learnable | "Background in learning sciences, cognitive science, HCI ... (formal or self-directed)" — self-directed is allowed |
| 6+ years shipping web products | Missing, structural | "6+ years building and shipping web products, with deep expertise across the stack" |
| Portfolio of interaction designs | Missing, structural (partially buildable) | "A portfolio showcasing innovative interaction designs" — real artefacts in Tier 2 shrink this |
| Strategy, cross-team influence, prioritization | Missing, structural (behavioral) | "Shaping team strategy, building conviction across cross-functional stakeholders" — answer from project leadership she genuinely has |

Education is not a gap: she holds a BE and an MS, satisfying the Bachelor's minimum and the relevant-field requirement.

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **TypeScript fundamentals.** What: types, interfaces, generics, strict mode, how it differs from Java/C#. Resource: the official TypeScript Handbook (typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook). Self-check: explain structural typing vs. C# nominal typing in 2 minutes, then type a small JSON API response without looking anything up.
2. **React mental model.** What: components, props/state, hooks, rendering. Resource: react.dev "Learn React" (Quick Start + Thinking in React). Self-check: sketch a component tree for a chat interface on paper and explain when state should lift up.
3. **The JD's own vocabulary: capability over engagement.** What: be ready to argue against "time-on-site" metrics. Resource: Anthropic's mission/research page (anthropic.com/research) plus the JD itself. Self-check: give three ways to measure that a user got *more capable*, not more active.
4. **A/B testing basics.** What: hypothesis, randomization, significance, novelty effects. Resource: Evan Miller's "How Not to Run an A/B Test". Self-check: explain why peeking at results early inflates false positives.
5. **HCI crash vocabulary.** What: cognitive load, scaffolding, deliberate practice, transfer. Resource: free chapters of Don Norman's *Design of Everyday Things* summaries via the Interaction Design Foundation's open literature. Self-check: apply "scaffolding" to one feature idea for Claude in education.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **React + TypeScript practice app.** Rebuild a small interactive UI (flashcard trainer or prompt playground). Proof artefact: a public GitHub repo with a README explaining component decisions.
2. **Motion and polish.** CSS transitions, spring physics, view transitions. Resource: Josh Comeau's free CSS/animation articles. Proof artefact: a single demo page with three polished micro-interactions, deployed on GitHub Pages.
3. **Claude API in production patterns.** What: streaming, tool use, prompt caching, evals. Resource: Anthropic's official docs (docs.anthropic.com). Proof artefact: a short written walkthrough, "How I'd build a capability-building tutor on the Claude API," in the repo.
4. **Capability-growth analytics.** What: define a metric for skill gain (pre/post task performance, hint-independence over time) and how to A/B test it. Proof artefact: a Jupyter notebook on synthetic user data computing a simple capability-growth metric.
5. **One learning-science deep dive.** What: deliberate practice and desirable difficulties (Bjork). plan.summary: BD's Engr 3 Hardware Test role probes reliability statistics (DOE, Weibull, Gage R&R, FMEA) and automated DAQ test-system design — areas where she has the programming foundation (LabVIEW, Python, Arduino, NI TestStand) but not the statistical-test-method layer. The plan front-loads reliability/DOE vocabulary for the screening call, then builds toward proof artefacts: a Weibull analysis notebook, a Gage R&R study, and a small 'not built yet' accelerated-life test rig, while the 5-year experience and mentoring requirements are treated as structural gaps with honest interview answers.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| LabVIEW programming ("Strong LabVIEW programming background") | Have | Core automation tool for DAQ and test sequences |
| NI TestStand / test automation | Have | Automated sequences and benchmark programs |
| Python, SQL ("Programming or scripting experience") | Have | Data aggregation, trending, reporting |
| Arduino / microcontrollers, SPI/I2C/UART, PID control | Have | "Improve or develop PLC- and microcontroller-based systems" |
| Verification and validation (V&V) | Have | PQPs, verification protocols |
| DOE ("full/fractional factorial, screening, response surface") | Missing, learnable | Characterize system performance, set design margins |
| ANOVA, regression, capability analysis (Cp/Cpk), hypothesis testing | Missing, learnable | Analyze DOE results in "Minitab, Python, or JMP" |
| MSA / Gage R&R ("Demonstrated experience... Gage R&R") | Missing, learnable | Prove test methods are repeatable before studies |
| Weibull / life data analysis ("MTBF/MCBF, hazard and survival plots, censored data") | Missing, learnable | Quantify reliability growth in life testing |
| FMEA, fault tree, 5-Why, 8D | Missing, learnable | Failure analysis and root-cause investigation |
| PLCs, motion control, NI DAQ hardware | Missing, learnable (PLC/DAQ hardware) | "Integrated DAQ systems for sensors, motion control" |
| Reliability sample-size / confidence-level judgment | Missing, learnable | Defend test plans to stakeholders |
| "Minimum experience of 5 years in a similar role" | Missing, structural | Seniority requirement; cannot be learned in weeks |
| "Experience mentoring, coaching, or technically leading" | Missing, structural | This is an Engr 3 / mentor role |
| Hands-on electro-mechanical fixture design (CAD, 45-lb lab work, on-site 4 days/wk) | Missing, structural | Physical lab presence and mechanical build experience |
| Never-claim list | Never-claim | None of these appear in the JD; nothing to add. Nothing from this plan goes on the resume |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **DOE vocabulary**: factors, levels, responses, blocking, randomization, full vs. fractional factorial, screening vs. response surface. Resource: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Ch. 5. Self-check: in 30 min, design on paper a 2^3 factorial for motor-torque vs. temperature vs. duty cycle, name the aliasing risk in a half-fraction.
2. **Gage R&R / MSA**: repeatability vs. reproducibility, %study variation, crossed vs. nested. Resource: Minitab's free support pages on Gage R&R. Self-check: explain in 2 minutes why a bad measurement system invalidates a DOE, and what %GR&R threshold is acceptable.
3. **Weibull basics**: shape/scale parameters, beta interpretation, MTBF vs. MCBF, censored data. Resource: ReliaWiki (ReliaSoft's public wiki), Weibull analysis chapters. Self-check: sketch a hazard plot by hand and state what beta > 1 means for wear-out.
4. **FMEA / fault tree / 8D**: severity-occurrence-detection scoring, RPN, AND/OR gates. Resource: ASQ's free FMEA and 8D overview pages. Self-check: build a 5-row FMEA table for a syringe-pump jam failure.
5. **PLC and motion-control fundamentals**: ladder logic basics, stepper/servo control loops (she has PID — extend it). Resource: NI's free "DAQ and motion control fundamentals" tutorials. Self-check: describe how she'd automate cycle counting on a life-test stand.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **DOE executed in Python** (JD allows "Minitab, Python, or JMP"): pyDOE3 + statsmodels ANOVA/regression on a simulated electro-mechanical response. Artefact: Jupyter notebook running a fractional-factorial DOE end-to-end with residual checks and capability output (Cp/Cpk).
2. **Weibull life-data analysis**: the `reliability` Python library on a censored dataset (generate or use public bearing-life data). Artefact: notebook producing Weibull fits, hazard/survival plots, MTBF with confidence bounds, and a one-page "reliability growth" memo.
3. **Gage R&R study**: design a crossed GR&R (3 operators x 10 parts x 3 trials) in Python, compute %GR&R and ndc. Artefact: script + written interpretation she could defend as an MSA plan.
4. **LabVIEW DAQ depth**: DAQmx acquisition with logging, fault detection, and unattended-run error handling; TestStand sequence calling it. Artefact: small LabVIEW/TestStand repo simulating an automated life-cycle test with cycle counting and a fault-injection demo.
5. **Medical-device V&V context**: how PQPs, traceability, and ISO 13485 / ISO 14971 shape test protocols at a company like BD. Artefact: 1-2 page walkthrough mapping a sample PQP to reliability tests, sampling plan, and acceptance criteria.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has no automated reliability/life-test project; the JD centers on one. **Not built yet.**
- Goal: desktop accelerated-life test stand for a small DC motor or solenoid.
- Data: cycle counts, current draw, temperature, vibration; run-to-failure with right-censoring.
- Stack: ESP32/Arduino rig control + sensors (she has these), LabVIEW or Python DAQ/logging, `reliability` library for analysis.
- Features: unattended run, automatic fault detection and shutdown, CSV logging.
- Evaluation: Weibull fit on failure data, MTBF with confidence interval, short FMEA of the rig itself.
- Deliverable: repo with wiring diagram, firmware, DAQ code, analysis notebook, 2-page test report.
- Hours: ~30-40 across weeks 2-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- 5 years: "I don't have five years in a dedicated test role. What I bring is hands-on LabVIEW, embedded, and Python automation, and I've spent the last month building exactly the reliability toolkit this role uses — I'd rather show you that work than stretch my history."
- Mentoring: "I haven't formally managed engineers, but I've taught teammates instrumentation and debugging informally, and the statistical-rigor coaching this role describes is something I've been preparing for deliberately."
- Fixture/CAD: "My strength is the automation and data side; mechanical fixture CAD is where I'd lean on your mechanical engineers early and learn fast."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: For Nuro's New Grad SWE (Routing) role, her registered skills already cover the core: C++, Python, PostgreSQL, AWS, CI/CD, streaming (Kafka/MQTT), and graph-search fundamentals via her Pacman project; the genuine prep work is TypeScript/React vocabulary, routing-at-scale algorithms, map data, ETA analytics, traffic simulation, and learn-only items (React, gRPC, Kubernetes) that may be learned but never claimed. The plan below is a 6-week, 11-item schedule ending in concrete artefacts: a mini routing engine repo, an ETA-accuracy notebook, a SUMO simulation walkthrough, and one 'not built yet' full-stack fleet-routing dashboard.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| React | Never-claim (learn ok, never assert) | "design, build, and ship full-stack applications using React, TypeScript" |
| TypeScript | Learnable | same JD line |
| C++ | Have (registered) | "software modules written in C++ that operate onboard the vehicle" |
| Graph/search fundamentals | Have (Pacman Search Algorithms project) | "routing algorithms... graph data structures" |
| Routing at scale (contraction hierarchies, time-dependent routing) | Learnable | "optimizing routing algorithms and understanding road network graphs" |
| Map data (OSM-style road graphs) | Learnable | "receive live map updates" |
| ETA/monitoring analytics | Learnable (Grafana, Pandas registered) | "monitoring and analytics infrastructure that supports routing performance and ETA accuracy" |
| Traffic simulation | Learnable | "simulation tools that shape the company's strategy for robot deployment" |
| Microservices design | Learnable (Flask, Docker, design patterns registered) | "designing microservices" |
| REST APIs, PostgreSQL, AWS, CI/CD, streaming | Have (Flask, PostgreSQL, AWS, CI/CD, Kafka, MQTT) | "RESTful or gRPC APIs", "relational databases", "cloud infrastructure", "Pub/Sub, streaming pipelines" |
| gRPC / Protocol Buffers | Never-claim (learn ok) | Bonus: "Experience with Protocol Buffers and gRPC" |
| Kubernetes | Never-claim (learn ok) | Bonus: "Exposure to Kubernetes" |
| Production onboard-vehicle software | Structural | "operate onboard the vehicle... interface with motion planning" |
| Bachelor's in CS-related field | Have (education; never a gap) | Minimum Qualifications |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **TypeScript fundamentals** — JD: "React, TypeScript, and modern web development practices". Learn: type annotations, interfaces, generics, tsconfig strict mode. Resource: the official TypeScript Handbook (typescriptlang.org/docs). Self-check: convert a 100-line JS file to strict TS with zero `any` in 30 minutes.
2. **Routing algorithm vocabulary** — JD: "optimizing routing algorithms". She has A*/Dijkstra from Pacman; add contraction hierarchies and time-dependent routing. Resource: OSRM's public docs/wiki on routing at scale. Self-check: explain in one paragraph, unaided, why plain Dijkstra is too slow at country scale and how CH fixes it.
3. **Map data basics** — JD: "road network graphs", "live map updates". Learn OSM nodes/ways/tags and how a routable graph is built. Resource: OpenStreetMap Beginners' Guide (wiki.openstreetmap.org). Self-check: download a city extract and count routable ways by highway tag.
4. **gRPC/Protobuf concepts (learn-only)** — JD bonus: "Protocol Buffers and gRPC". Learn service definitions, message types, unary vs streaming RPCs. Resource: grpc.io "What is gRPC?" Self-check: write a `.proto` for a RouteService with a streaming ETA method from memory.
5. **React mental model (learn-only)** — JD: "frontend architecture decisions, component libraries". Learn components, props, hooks, state lifting. Resource: react.dev "Learn React". Self-check: build a small counter-plus-list app unaided and explain useEffect dependencies out loud.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Mini routing engine.** Python or C++ over an OSM extract: build the road graph, implement Dijkstra and A* with haversine heuristic, benchmark runtime vs graph size. Artefact: public GitHub repo with README containing benchmark tables.
2. **ETA accuracy study.** Simulate predicted vs realized travel times on 100 origin-destination pairs; compute MAE/MAPE by time-of-day; discuss why ETA accuracy matters (JD: "more accurate ETAs"). Artefact: Jupyter notebook with charts and a written error analysis.
3. **Fleet traffic simulation.** Build a SUMO scenario with 10-50 delivery vehicles; measure fleet throughput and ETA drift under congestion. Artefact: repo with scenario configs plus a one-page written walkthrough of findings.
4. **gRPC demo service (learn-only).** Small Python RouteService defined in protobuf with server-streaming ETA updates and a demo client. Artefact: small repo; stays off the resume.
5. **Microservices decomposition doc.** Take her existing Medical IoT platform and write a design doc splitting it into microservices with API contracts, failure modes, and tradeoffs (JD: "instinct for making the right tradeoffs"). Artefact: written design doc she can walk an interviewer through.

## Build-now project — not built yet

**Fleet routing ops dashboard (full-stack).** Goal: a small end-to-end app echoing Routing-team work — request routes, view ETAs, watch simulated vehicles. Data: one OSM city extract plus simulated vehicle telemetry (reuse her Kafka/MQTT streaming experience). Stack: TypeScript + React frontend (learning exercise), Flask API (Have), PostgreSQL (Have), Docker Compose (Have). Features: map view of computed routes, ETA table, live simulated positions via server-sent events. Evaluation: 100 random OD pairs routed correctly; ETA error stats displayed; API p95 under 300 ms. Deliverable: public repo, README with screenshots, 3-minute demo video. Effort: roughly 40-50 hours across weeks 3-6. Note: React output here is learning evidence only and remains never-claim.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- "I haven't shipped software that runs on a real vehicle. What I do have is embedded C and C++ on FPGAs and microcontrollers, including an FPGA-based autonomous vehicle project, so I'm comfortable with resource-constrained, deterministic code — and I'm eager to learn your onboard stack."
- "My systems experience is coursework and personal projects, not production scale. I bring TDD habits and end-to-end ownership, and I plan to close the production gap fast through code review and mentorship."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — and never-claim skills (React, gRPC, Kubernetes) never go on the resume at all.

plan.summary: The JD's core backend requirements (Java/Python/C++, DS&A, REST, Kafka, Docker, AWS, observability) are already covered by her registered skills, so the plan concentrates on the genuinely missing layer: production distributed-infrastructure patterns (rate limiting, circuit breaking, feature flags, config hot-reload, traffic replay, distributed tracing) plus honest framing of her lack of production-at-scale operating experience. Redis, Elasticsearch, Go and several other JD-adjacent terms are on her never-claim list and are treated strictly as learn-only, never as resume or interview claims.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| "programming fundamentals in at least one backend language such as Java... Python, C++" | Have (Java, Python, C++ all registered) | Daily implementation language |
| "data structures, algorithms, and object-oriented design" | Have (Design patterns, Pacman Search coursework) | New-grad interview core |
| "building RESTful APIs/services, request/response handling, error handling" | Have (Flask, Expense Tracker project) | Service development |
| "event streaming" / "Kafka... is a plus" | Have (Apache Kafka, Medical IoT Analytics) | Their event backbone |
| "containers, and cloud platforms" | Have (Docker, EC2/S3/Lambda, Linux) | Deploy/runtime substrate |
| "concurrency... scalability, caching, messaging" | Partially have (Multithreading, Kafka); distributed-systems depth missing | Core infra design |
| "rate limiting and circuit breaking", "feature flags and A/B testing", "distributed configuration management and hot reloading", "traffic capture and replay" | Missing, learnable 3-6 weeks | The actual services this team builds |
| "distributed logging, tracing, monitoring, and alerting" | Partially have (Grafana); OpenTelemetry/tracing missing | Observability mandate |
| "distributed key value store, schema-less data store" | Partially have (MongoDB); internals (consensus, partitioning) missing | Storage-layer ownership |
| "operating... open source technologies like Kafka, Elasticsearch or Opensearch, Istio" | Kafka Have; Elasticsearch/Opensearch Never-claim; Istio learnable conceptually (needs k8s, which is never-claim) | Ops maturity signal |
| "Go" | Never-claim (she has Java/Python/C++; JD says "such as") | Team language |
| "Redis" (implied by KV store/rate limiting) | Never-claim — learn, never claim | Common implementation choice |
| Operating production infra at scale ("designing and operating reliable and resilient foundational services") | Structural — years of production/on-call experience | What separates new grads from infra veterans |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Distributed-systems vocabulary.** Consistency, partitioning, replication, consensus (Raft at concept level), CAP. Resource: the free System Design Primer (github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer). Self-check: in 30 min, whiteboard from memory how you'd scale a key-value store and what breaks first.
2. **Rate limiting & circuit breaking** (JD lists both verbatim). Token bucket vs. sliding window; breaker states. Resource: free sections of the "Rate Limiting" and "Circuit Breaker" chapters on patterns.ambig.com / Microsoft Azure architecture center docs. Self-check: explain a breaker state diagram and where it sits relative to retries.
3. **Feature flags & A/B testing mechanics** (JD: "system for feature flags and A/B testing"). Targeting, gradual rollout, kill switches. Resource: OpenFeature docs (openfeature.dev). Self-check: describe a flag-based canary rollout and its rollback path in 5 sentences.
4. **Config management & hot reload** (JD verbatim). Push vs. pull, versioning, consistency. Resource: free etcd and Consul intro docs. Self-check: sketch two designs for hot-reloading config to 1,000 services.
5. **Microservice metrics** (JD: "methodologies and metrics to measure performance"). RED/USE methods, p50/p99, SLI/SLO. Resource: Google SRE book, free online (sre.google/sre-book), Monitoring chapter. Self-check: define an SLO for a login API and pick its SLIs.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry** (JD: "distributed logging, tracing"). Instrument a two-service Flask app, propagate trace context, export to Jaeger via Docker. Artefact: small repo with docker-compose, instrumented services, screenshots of a trace waterfall.
2. **Traffic capture & replay** (JD verbatim). Study goreplay/mitmproxy; build a replay harness that records requests to one Flask service and replays against a shadow instance. Artefact: repo with replay script + a short README on fidelity pitfalls (side effects, non-idempotency).
3. **KV-store internals.** LSM vs. B-tree, WAL, partitioning. Resource: free CMU 15-445 lectures (YouTube). Artefact: written walkthrough (~800 words) of how a write flows through an LSM store.
4. **Kafka depth beyond her project.** Consumer groups, rebalancing, exactly-once, lag monitoring. Resource: free Kafka docs design section. Artefact: notebook/gist demonstrating consumer-lag alerting logic against her Medical IoT pipeline.
5. **Interview algorithm reps.** Distributed-infra-flavored problems (LRU cache, rate limiter, design a URL shortener). Resource: NeetCode free list. Artefact: 25 solved problems with notes in a repo.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has no project that is *infra services themselves* — her projects consume infrastructure rather than build it, and this JD builds it. Spec (label: **not built yet**):
- **Goal:** a mini "platform services" repo: feature-flag service + rate limiter + traffic replay harness.
- **Data:** synthetic HTTP request logs generated by a load script.
- **Stack:** Python/Flask, Docker Compose, Kafka (Have), OpenTelemetry; no Kubernetes, Redis, Go (never-claim).
- **Evaluation:** p99 latency under 2x load with limiter on vs. off; flag rollout rollback demo.
- **Deliverable:** public repo with README architecture diagram and load-test numbers.
- **Hours:** ~25 across weeks 3-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- On production scale: "I haven't operated infrastructure at Moveworks' scale yet — my Kafka and AWS work is project-scale. What I can show is that I've studied the failure modes and built small versions of the services this team runs."
- On Go/Elasticsearch: "My daily languages are Java, Python and C++, and my search experience is limited; I pick up new stacks quickly and I'm already working through the concepts."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after each item is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: The OpenAI Quality & Developer Tools role maps well onto her registered skills (Python, C, C++, Linux, embedded, CI/CD, test automation), so the plan concentrates on the genuinely new ground: Buildkite, hardware-in-the-loop lab orchestration, flake detection/quarantine, systemd/udev depth, and release-gate metrics. Tier 1 builds screening-call vocabulary on CI promotion and HIL concepts; Tier 2 produces proof artefacts; the HIL orchestrator project fills the missing hardware-lab project type.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python, C, C++ | Have | "proficient in Python, C, C++, or Rust" |
| Linux, Git, Docker, CI/CD | Have | "strong Linux fundamentals", "building CI/CD pipelines" |
| Test automation, TDD, NI TestStand | Have | "deep experience building software quality, test automation" |

| Grafana, Streamlit | Have (adjacent) | "dashboards and alerts for pass rates" |
| Buildkite | Missing, learnable | "Integrate test suites with Buildkite, enforce promotion criteria" |
| Hardware-in-the-loop lab design | Missing, learnable (conceptually) | "designing and operating hardware-in-the-loop labs and device orchestration" |
| Flake detection & quarantine | Missing, learnable | "detect and quarantine flaky tests; drive root-cause analysis" |
| systemd/udev depth | Missing, learnable | "strong Linux fundamentals, including... udev/systemd" |
| Release gates, staged rollout/rollback | Missing, learnable | "promotion criteria for staging and production", "staged rollouts, and rollback/forward strategies" |
| Rust | Never-claim | Listed as alternative language; on her never-claim list — learn basics, never assert proficiency |
| HIL labs "at scale", hardware shipped at scale | Structural | "demonstrated success... at scale" — years of production lab operation |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Buildkite pipeline model** — JD: "Integrate test suites with Buildkite." Learn agents, pipelines-as-YAML, steps, artifacts, test analytics. Resource: Buildkite official docs (buildkite.com/docs) Quickstart + Test Analytics guides. Self-check (30 min): sketch a 3-stage pipeline (unit -> integration -> HIL gate) on paper with promotion conditions, and explain each step aloud.
2. **udev/systemd fundamentals** — JD: "processes, networking, storage, and udev/systemd." Learn unit files, targets, journald, and how udev rules map a plugged-in device to a /dev node. Resource: freedesktop.org systemd man pages (systemd.unit, udev(7)). Self-check: write a udev rule that names a USB serial device consistently and a systemd service that starts a logger on boot; explain both without notes.
3. **Flaky-test vocabulary** — JD: "flake detection and quarantine, signal-quality guardrails." Learn: quarantine tags, rerun budgets, flake rate dashboards, bisection. Resource: Google's Testing Blog, "Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them." Self-check: define flake rate, quarantine SLA, and three root-cause classes from memory.
4. **Release gating concepts** — JD: "enforce promotion criteria", "staged rollouts, and rollback/forward." Learn canary/staged rollout, rollback vs roll-forward, artifact traceability. Resource: Martin Fowler, "ContinuousDelivery" and "CanaryRelease" articles. Self-check: argue rollback vs roll-forward for a firmware regression in 5 sentences.
5. **HIL lab anatomy** — JD: "racks, power and networking systems, and orchestration for device testing." Learn: PDUs, network switches, device under test (DUT), flashing/provisioning loops, telemetry capture. Resource: "Hardware-in-the-Loop Testing" overview articles + NI HIL documentation. Self-check: draw a rack diagram and walk the flash-test-telemetry cycle.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Buildkite pipeline repo** — Build a real pipeline for one existing project (e.g., the Medical IoT platform): unit tests, artifact upload, a promotion gate using Buildkite's block step. Artefact: public repo with `pipeline.yml`, screenshots of a green run and a blocked promotion.
2. **Flake-quarantine harness** — Write a pytest plugin/script that reruns failures N times, tags flaky tests, emits a flake-rate report, and auto-excludes quarantined tests. Artefact: repo + sample HTML/markdown flake report run against deliberately flaky tests she seeds.
3. **Device-flashing orchestrator prototype** — Script (Python + pyserial/adb-style) that provisions and flashes an ESP32 over UART, runs a smoke test, and captures logs/telemetry with timestamps. Artefact: repo with README walkthrough and a captured log showing flash -> test -> report.
4. **Quality-signals dashboard** — Grafana (registered skill) dashboard fed by a tiny pipeline-results database: pass rate, flake rate, mean time to triage, release-readiness flag. Artefact: dashboard JSON + screenshot set + one-page note on which metrics gate a release.
5. **systemd/udev hands-on lab** — A systemd-managed test-runner service with automatic device attach via udev rule, journald logging, and restart policy. Artefact: short written walkthrough (markdown) with the unit file, udev rule, and journalctl output.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

Her projects include embedded/IoT work but no CI/CD pipeline or device-orchestration project she built end-to-end; the JD demands both ("CI/CD integration & releases", "device orchestration"). **Not built yet.**

- Goal: mini hardware-in-the-loop orchestrator + release gate for one ESP32.
- Data: synthetic firmware builds; test results stored in SQLite/PostgreSQL.
- Stack: Python, ESP32 (registered), Buildkite free tier or self-hosted agent, Grafana.
- Flow: commit -> Buildkite builds firmware -> flashes ESP32 via orchestrator -> runs UART smoke tests -> results to DB -> flake detector -> Grafana dashboard -> promotion gate blocks on failures.
- Evaluation: repro run 20x; flake rate reported; one seeded bug auto-caught.
- Deliverable: public repo, README walkthrough, screenshots of gated release.
- Hours: ~35-45 across weeks 2-5 (this is the Tier 2 items 1-4 wired together).

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- HIL labs at scale: "I've built and flashed embedded devices hands-on and I understand lab anatomy — racks, provisioning, telemetry. I haven't operated a multi-rack lab at production scale, and I'd ramp on your existing lab quickly because the orchestration concepts are ones I've been practicing."
- Shipped hardware at scale: "My embedded work has been project and prototype scale, not a mass-shipped product line. What transfers directly is test automation, flashing/provisioning, and debugging across software and firmware — the rest I'm prepared to learn fast."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: For Twilio's Software Engineer - Voice Trust role, most hard requirements (Java, Kafka, AWS, CI/CD, Grafana, AI-assisted coding) are already registered skills; the plan targets the real gaps: Prometheus/Datadog observability depth, SQS, caching patterns, SIP and STIR/SHAKEN protocol literacy, and honest framing of the structural gaps (2-3+ years production JVM, on-call, proven scale). One build-now project — a small Java real-time service with Kafka, Prometheus metrics and CI/CD — supplies the proof artefact the technical round will probe.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Java / JVM, 2-3+ yrs large-scale distributed | Structural | "Minimum 2-3+ years of hands-on experience... on JVM based technologies" |
| RESTful services, API design | Have (Flask projects) | "Experience building RESTful services, API design" |
