| AWS (EC2/S3/RDS/Lambda/Glue/EMR) | Have | "cloud infrastructures such as AWS, GCP..." |
| Grafana | Have | "monitoring/alerting tools (Prometheus, Datadog, Grafana)" |
| Prometheus, Datadog | Missing, learnable | Same line; metrics/alerts are how Voice Trust proves reliability |
| On-call, incident response | Structural | "Experience with on-call rotations, incident response" |
| AI coding assistants + evaluating AI code | Have (Prompt engineering, LangChain) | "Demonstrated proficiency working with AI coding assistants... show examples" |
| CS fundamentals, Bachelor's degree | Have (MS, University of Arkansas; degrees never gaps) | "Strong Computer Science fundamentals... Bachelor's degree" |
| SQL/NoSQL scaling, caching | Partially Have (PostgreSQL, MongoDB); caching patterns learnable; Redis = Never-claim | "scaling data tiers employing a variety of SQL/NoSQL database and caching technologies" |
| Horizontally-scalable production backends | Structural | "proven ability to design and develop horizontally-scalable, resilient... systems" |
| SIP protocol | Missing, learnable (fundamentals) | "Knowledge and experience working with SIP protocol" |
| STIR/SHAKEN | Missing, learnable (fundamentals) | "Knowledge and experience working with Stir/Shaken protocol" — core to Voice Trust's caller-ID mission |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **SIP essentials** — the role is Voice; learn sessions, INVITE/ACK/BYE, REGISTER, response codes, SDP basics. Resource: RFC 3261 (sections 1-13) plus Twilio's own SIP docs. Self-check: in 30 min, draw a call-setup ladder diagram and explain a 487 vs 486 response aloud.
2. **STIR/SHAKEN** — this team's reason to exist ("ensure their customers will answer their calls"). Learn attestation levels A/B/C, PASSporT tokens, certificates. Resource: FCC STIR/SHAKEN overview + ATIS-1000074 summary. Self-check: explain in writing, in 5 sentences, why SHAKEN needs a certificate authority.
3. **SQS vs Kafka mental model** — she has Kafka; learn SQS semantics (at-least-once, visibility timeout, FIFO vs standard, DLQs). Resource: AWS SQS Developer Guide core sections. Self-check: 30-min written comparison of when you'd pick SQS over Kafka for call-event processing.
4. **Prometheus data model** — metrics types, labels, PromQL basics, alert rules. Resource: prometheus.io "Overview" + "Querying basics". Self-check: write 5 PromQL queries against a demo endpoint and explain each.
5. **On-call vocabulary** — SLOs/SLIs, error budgets, incident severity, postmortems, so she can discuss the on-call requirement honestly. Resource: Google SRE book, chapters "Embracing Risk" and "Postmortem Culture" (free online). Self-check: write a mock postmortem for a past project bug.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Prometheus + Grafana on a real service** — instrument a small HTTP service with counters/histograms, build a dashboard, set one alert. Artefact: public repo with docker-compose (app + Prometheus + Grafana), a dashboard JSON, and screenshots; Docker and Grafana are registered skills. Reacting to: "monitoring/alerting tools (Prometheus, Datadog, Grafana)".
2. **Low-latency Java service design** — the JD demands "high throughput and low latency". Learn JVM GC basics (G1), connection pooling, backpressure, p99 thinking. Artefact: a written walkthrough (markdown doc) of load-testing a Java endpoint with `wrk`, showing latency percentiles before/after tuning.
3. **Distributed-systems design reps** — idempotency, retries with jitter, circuit breakers, horizontal scaling. Resource: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" chapters 1-8 or the free System Design Primer (GitHub). Artefact: a one-page design doc for a rate-limited call-routing API, written as detailed prose — Twilio explicitly values "detailed prose".
4. **AI-assisted workflow evidence** — the JD says "describe your workflows and show examples" and "demonstrate with metrics". Artefact: a short written walkthrough of building one Tier-2 artefact with an AI assistant: prompts used, what she rejected and why (correctness, security), rough time saved.
5. **SIP hands-on** — parse a real SIP trace. Artefact: a notebook or markdown walkthrough annotating a captured INVITE-to-BYE exchange header by header, including how STIR/SHAKEN Identity headers attach.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has no production-style Java backend project; her portfolio is ML, IoT and embedded. **Not built yet.** Spec: Goal — a "call-event ingest" service mimicking Voice Trust's shape. Data — synthetic call records (call SID, from/to, SIP code, attestation level). Stack — Java (registered) REST API, Kafka (registered) as the event bus, PostgreSQL (registered) storage, Prometheus metrics + Grafana (registered) dashboard, GitHub Actions CI/CD (registered). Evaluation — a wrk load test showing throughput and p99 latency, plus one triggered alert. Deliverable — public repo: service, docker-compose, dashboard JSON, CI logs, README design doc. Hours — roughly 25-35 across weeks 2-5. No never-claim technology is used.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **2-3+ years production JVM**: "My Java experience is real but project-scale, not multi-year production. I've been closing that deliberately — here's a low-latency service I built and load-tested, and here's what I learned about the JVM under pressure."
- **On-call / incident response**: "I haven't carried a pager in production. I have owned failures end-to-end on my own systems — here's a postmortem I wrote — and I've studied SRE incident practice so I can be useful in a rotation from week one."
- **Proven horizontal scale**: "I understand the patterns — statelessness, backpressure, idempotent consumers — and can walk you through applying them, but I won't claim production scale I haven't run."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after it is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered.

plan.summary: She already covers most of VUMC's must-haves (Databricks, Python, SQL, Docker, CI/CD); the real prep is Databricks platform administration at scale, Terraform, PowerShell, and Azure-native depth, all learnable in 3-6 weeks. ## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Databricks workspace administration vocabulary** (JD: "compute policies, access controls, and governance"). Learn: workspaces vs. clusters, cluster policies, instance pools, PATs vs. service principals, Unity Catalog basics. Resource: Microsoft Learn "Azure Databricks administration" learning path (free). Self-check: explain to a friend, without notes, how you'd stop a team from launching oversized clusters.
2. **Terraform fundamentals** (JD: "Infrastructure as Code solutions such as Terraform"). Learn: providers, plan/apply, state, modules. Resource: HashiCorp's free "Terraform: Get Started - Azure" tutorial. Self-check: write and `terraform plan` a config that creates one Azure resource group; say honestly: "learning it now, never run it in production."
3. **PowerShell basics** (JD bonus). Learn: cmdlets, pipes, scripting loops, Az module. Resource: Microsoft Learn "Automate administrative tasks with PowerShell" (free). Self-check: write a 20-line script that lists files over 100MB and logs them.
4. **GitHub Actions CI/CD mechanics** (JD: "CI/CD automation in GitLab, GitHub, or Azure DevOps"). Learn: workflows, jobs, runners, secrets, environments. Resource: GitHub's official "Understanding GitHub Actions" docs. Self-check: sketch a workflow that lints and tests on push, deploys on tag.
5. **Azure Databricks cost model** (JD: "monitoring performance and costs"). Learn: DBUs, cluster autoscaling vs. pools, serverless vs. classic compute, budget alerts. Resource: Databricks free edition + "cost management" docs. Self-check: answer "why did our bill double?" with three plausible causes and how you'd prove each.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Cluster policies and access control in practice.** Build policies restricting instance types and spot usage; map groups to entitlements. Artefact: a small repo with JSON cluster policy definitions plus a README explaining the guardrails and why.
2. **Terraform with the Databricks provider.** Provision a workspace-level setup: cluster policy, job, service principal. Artefact: GitHub repo `databricks-terraform-lab` with `main.tf`, variables, and a recorded `plan` output walkthrough.
3. **CI/CD pipeline for a Databricks job.** GitHub Actions workflow that runs pytest, validates notebooks with `databricks bundle validate`, and deploys on merge. Artefact: the repo's Actions tab showing green runs plus a short written walkthrough of the YAML.
4. **Platform health and cost monitoring.** System tables (`system.billing.usage`, `system.access.audit`) queried in a notebook; cost-per-workspace dashboard. Artefact: a notebook + one-page write-up of findings on her own free-tier workspace.
5. **REST ingestion pipeline, hardened** (JD: "variety of source systems - flat files, APIs, databases"). Python OOP pipeline pulling a public API into Delta Lake with retries, schema checks, and logging. Artefact: repo with tests and a run log.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

**"Mini platform admin kit" - not built yet.** The JD's center of gravity (IaC + CI/CD for Databricks, self-built) matches no project she has. Goal: automate provisioning and monitoring of a small Databricks environment the way VUMC runs its 100+. Data: NYC taxi open dataset as the payload. Stack: Terraform (Databricks + Azure providers), GitHub Actions, Databricks free edition, system tables, Python/pytest. Evaluation: `terraform apply` from clean state in under 15 min; CI pipeline blocks a deploy when a cluster policy is violated; cost notebook shows per-job DBU spend. Deliverable: public GitHub repo with README architecture diagram, Actions history, and a 2-page ops runbook. Hours: 30-40 across weeks 2-5. This satisfies the JD's "link to your GitHub profile" bonus directly.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **100+ workspace scale:** "I've built pipelines on Databricks and I'm now deep into its admin surface - policies, governance, cost controls. I haven't operated a platform at your scale yet, which is exactly why this role appeals to me; I'd want to earn that under your senior engineers."
- **Healthcare domain:** "I haven't worked with clinical data or under HIPAA, but my medical IoT project taught me to treat sensitive telemetry carefully, and I'd complete VUMC's compliance training before touching anything."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after it is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered.

plan.summary: Most of the JD's named stack (Python, C#, SQL, MongoDB, SQL Server, MQTT, Grafana, Docker, Linux, embedded C) is already registered as Have; the real prep targets are automotive networking (OSI/TCP-IP, TCP/UDP), the CAN bus, Wireshark, MATLAB, and InfluxDB, all learnable in the 3-6 week window. Structural gaps — actual motorsport/Formula SAE experience, a year of industry application engineering, and hands-on HIL hardware time — need honest interview answers, not study plans.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python, C#, SQL, MongoDB, SQL Server | Have | "programming or scripting languages, such as Python, MATLAB, or C#"; "SQL Server, MongoDB, or InfluxDB" |
| MQTT, Grafana, Docker, Linux, AWS | Have | "Microsoft Azure, AWS, Kubernetes, MQTT, and Grafana"; "Linux or Windows command-line" |
| Embedded C, SPI/I2C/UART, test automation, V&V | Have | "embedded systems"; "Validate... requirements" |
| MATLAB | Learnable (3-6 wks) | named first in scripting languages |
| OSI / TCP-IP models, TCP/UDP/Ethernet/Wi-Fi/cellular | Learnable | "network communication frameworks, including the OSI and TCP/IP models" |
| CAN protocol | Learnable | "automotive communication protocols such as CAN and Ethernet" |
| Wireshark | Learnable | "diagnostic, or test tools such as Wireshark" |
| InfluxDB | Learnable | named time-series database for telemetry data |
| Reading electrical schematics | Learnable | "read and interpret electrical schematics" |
| HIL bench testing | Learnable concepts; real rig time structural | "Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) bench tests" |
| Professional/collegiate motorsport experience | Structural | "Experience in professional motorsport, significant collegiate racing (e.g., Formula SAE, EcoCAR)" |
| 1+ yrs industry application engineering | Structural | Required qualification; only real time counts |
| Powertrain / vehicle-level diagnostics depth | Structural (basics learnable) | "internal combustion, hybrid, and/or battery-electric vehicle systems" |
| Kubernetes | Never-claim | JD names it; on her never-claim list — learn privately if desired, never claim |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **OSI and TCP/IP models, TCP vs UDP** (JD: "OSI and TCP/IP models... TCP, UDP"). Learn the 7/4 layers, handshake vs datagram tradeoffs, why telemetry often rides UDP. Resource: Practical Networking's free YouTube "Networking Fundamentals" playlist. Self-check: in 30 minutes, draw both models from memory and explain aloud when UDP beats TCP for race telemetry.
2. **CAN bus fundamentals** (JD: "CAN"). Frame anatomy (ID, DLC, payload), arbitration, bit rates, OBD-II vs raw CAN. Resource: CSS Electronics' free "CAN Bus Explained" intro series. Self-check: hand-decode three sample CAN frames and say which node wins arbitration and why.
3. **Wireshark basics** (JD: "tools such as Wireshark"). Capture filters, display filters, TCP handshake and retransmission spotting. Resource: official Wireshark sample captures at wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures plus the user guide. Self-check: capture 5 minutes of local traffic, isolate a full TCP handshake, flag one retransmission, explain it.
4. **MATLAB fundamentals** (JD lists MATLAB first among languages). Arrays, plotting, data import, scripts vs functions. Resource: free MATLAB Onramp (MathWorks, ~2 hours). Self-check: load a CSV of sensor data, clean it, plot two channels, compute basic stats — timed, 30 minutes.
5. **Telemetry vocabulary + honest self-positioning** (JD: "telemetry gateway units", "trackside telemetry servers"). Learn the end-to-end path: ECU → CAN → gateway → radio/cellular → server → dashboard. Resource: Bosch Motorsport's public telemetry product pages. Self-check: deliver a 2-minute verbal walkthrough of that chain, ending with one honest sentence on where she personally stands.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Simulated CAN telemetry pipeline.** Use python-can with a virtual CAN interface to generate frames (rpm, speed, temps), publish over MQTT (registered), visualize in Grafana (registered). Artefact: a small public repo with README, docker-compose, and screenshots — a miniature of the JD's "telemetry gateway... data collection, analysis, and distribution."
2. **InfluxDB depth** (JD names it). Time-series schema, tags vs fields, retention, Flux queries. Artefact: extend the same repo to log the simulated CAN stream into InfluxDB, with a notebook comparing query patterns against her registered MongoDB approach.
3. **Networking troubleshooting walkthrough** (JD: "wired and wireless... Wi-Fi, and cellular"). Latency/packet-loss diagnosis with ping, traceroute, Wireshark; Wi-Fi vs cellular link budget intuition. Artefact: a written walkthrough of diagnosing a staged flaky-connection scenario, with captures attached.
4. **HIL-by-analogy bench rig** (JD: "HIL bench tests"). ESP32 (registered) as a stand-in ECU emitting sensor data; a Python test harness injecting faults and asserting behavior. Artefact: repo plus a one-page test report written like a V&V record — honest framing as a bench-test exercise, not real HIL.
5. **Vehicle systems literacy** (JD: "powertrain, chassis, or controls"). ICE vs hybrid vs BEV architecture at block-diagram level; how PID control (registered) maps to throttle/boost control. Resource: free chapters of the SAE "Automotive Engineering Fundamentals" summaries and Bosch's public mobility explainers. Artefact: a short written walkthrough connecting a control loop from her Elevator Control System project to an automotive control problem.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **Motorsport experience:** "I haven't raced or been on a Formula SAE team — I won't pretend otherwise. What I bring is embedded systems and real-time telemetry work, and since applying I've built a simulated CAN-to-Grafana pipeline so I can be useful trackside faster."
- **Industry application engineering year:** "My application-engineering exposure so far is academic and project-based — requirements, bench testing, and customer-style documentation — and I'm looking for this role to be where I convert that into industry experience."
- **HIL hardware time:** "I've practiced the closed-loop test discipline on a bench rig I built myself; real HIL rigs are exactly what I'm here to learn on."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before, and Kubernetes never.

sources.title: Bosch Group - Associate Motorsport Software Engineer (SmartRecruiters)

limitations: Registered skills are treated as Have per instructions, even where the genuine_gaps list (which contains mostly raw JD boilerplate text rather than true gaps) overlaps them; no independent verification of her actual proficiency was possible.
Project titles were provided without contents, so bucket placement relies on titles plus the registered skill list only.
Recommended resources are publicly documented free offerings; availability and pricing of free tiers can change.

The required '1+ years of experience' qualifications cannot be learned into existence in 3-6 weeks; the plan covers vocabulary and demonstrable analogues only, and the interview answers stay honest about that.
Kubernetes appears in the JD but is on the never-claim list, so it is excluded from the learning tiers and must never be asserted on the resume or in interviews.

plan.summary: Verkada's Imaging Systems role is an embedded C/C++ camera-stack job; she already holds the core (C++, C, Embedded C, Linux, CV, FPGA), so the genuine gaps are imaging-specific: 3A algorithms, ISP, optics/sensor knowledge, and IQ evaluation, plus structural gaps of 3+ years experience and vendor IQ tuning. The plan front-loads imaging vocabulary and fundamentals for the screening call, then hands-on libcamera/ISP work with proof artefacts before the technical round.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| C++, C, "systems programming" | Have | "primarily in C++ and C" across the imaging stack |
| Embedded Linux / IoT on-device software | Have (Embedded C, FreeRTOS, Linux, ESP32) | "on-device software for IoT systems or embedded Linux environments" |
| Computer vision collaboration | Have (Object detection/tracking, YOLO, PyTorch) | "partnering closely with ... computer vision teams" |
| 3A algorithms: AE, AF, AWB | Missing - learnable | Core of the role: "autofocus, auto-exposure, image quality" |
| ISP algorithms, image sensors, optics | Missing - learnable (fundamentals in 3-6 wks) | "Working knowledge of optics, image sensors, ISP algorithms" |
| WDR, day/night transition | Missing - learnable | Named camera features she must discuss |
| Objective/subjective IQ evaluation (noise, sharpness, color) | Missing - learnable | "evaluate image quality both objectively and subjectively" |
| Sensor drivers / camera pipeline config (V4L2, MIPI CSI-2) | Missing - learnable (fundamentals) | "camera pipeline configuration, sensor drivers" |
| Vendor IQ tuning, production triage | Missing - structural | Real tuning-tool and field experience takes years; learn concepts only |
| "3+ years of software development experience" | Missing - structural | Cannot be learned; answer with project depth honestly |
| Onsite 5 days/week (San Mateo) | Structural (logistics) | Hard requirement, not a skill |
| Never-claim list | Never-claim | None of the never-claim skills appear in this JD; no conflict |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **ISP pipeline overview** (Bayer, demosaic, black level, gamma, color correction) - react to "camera pipeline configuration". Resource: Raspberry Pi Camera Software libcamera docs (datasheets.raspberrypi.com). Self-check: draw the pipeline from photon to JPEG from memory in 30 min, label each block's failure mode.
2. **Auto-exposure fundamentals** (metering, exposure time vs gain, flicker). Resource: Cambridge in Colour "Camera Exposure" tutorial. Self-check: explain in 30 min why AE prefers gain over shutter at low light in security video, and what 50/60Hz flicker does to exposure steps.
3. **Autofocus types** (contrast-detection vs phase-detection, focus value curves). Resource: Cambridge in Colour autofocus tutorial. Self-check: sketch a contrast-AF hill-climbing search and name two ways it fails (low light, flat scenes).
4. **AWB basics** (gray world, white patch, color temperature). Resource: LearnOpenCV white-balance article (free). Self-check: explain why gray-world breaks on a single-color scene, in writing, 30 min.
5. **Vocabulary drill**: MIPI CSI-2, V4L2, WDR, ISP, IQ tuning, day/night IR-cut. Self-check: define each in one sentence and say honestly "I've studied this, not shipped it" for each.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Hands-on libcamera tuning** on a Raspberry Pi + camera module: edit the tuning JSON, capture before/after raw frames. Artefact: small repo with tuning file, paired images, and a README of what each change did.
2. **Implement a mini AE loop**: read raw frames (rawpy/libcamera), compute a metering statistic, adjust simulated exposure/gain to a target brightness. Artefact: Jupyter notebook with plots of convergence and a failure case (backlight).
3. **Implement AWB from scratch** (gray-world + white-patch) in Python or C++; compare against OpenCV's xphoto. Artefact: notebook with side-by-side images and a short write-up of when each method fails.
4. **Trace a real sensor driver**: read the Linux kernel imx219/imx477 V4L2 driver and the media-controller docs. Artefact: written walkthrough "how a frame gets from sensor to userspace on Linux," with the ioctl path annotated.
5. **Verkada-domain depth**: security-camera imaging constraints (low light, WDR scenes, IR day/night, edge AI on-device). Artefact: one-page written analysis of three hard imaging scenarios for security cameras and how 3A/ISP settings address each.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has embedded and CV projects but none on a camera imaging pipeline, so: **Mini ISP from raw sensor data** - *not built yet*. Goal: convert raw Bayer captures into viewable images with a self-built pipeline. Data: raw frames from a Raspberry Pi camera (DNG) or a public raw dataset. Stack: Python + NumPy for the pipeline (black-level, demosaic, AWB, CCM, gamma), C++ port of one hot path, libcamera for capture. Evaluation: objective metrics (SNR, color error vs a color-checker shot) plus subjective side-by-side against libcamera's own output. Deliverable: repo + notebook + one-page write-up. Hours: ~25-30 over weeks 3-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **3+ years / vendor IQ tuning**: "My imaging work so far is academic and self-directed - I've built the pipeline pieces myself and tuned on real hardware, but I haven't done production IQ tuning with a sensor vendor. That part I'd be learning from the team, and it's exactly why I want this role."

plan.summary: Twilio's Platform Engineering L2 role is unusually junior-friendly: the JD explicitly waives deep production Kubernetes experience and asks for fundamentals plus willingness to learn. The plan front-loads Kubernetes, Terraform, Shell/YAML, GitOps and Go basics before the screening call, then builds one small containerized deploy-and-observe project before the technical round; Kubernetes, Terraform and Go stay strictly in the learn bucket until mastered, since they are on the never-claim list.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Kubernetes (deployments, pods, services) | Never-claim -> learn | "basic Kubernetes operations (deployments, pods, services) is expected" |
| Terraform / IaC | Never-claim -> learn | "contribute to Terraform-based infrastructure automation" |
| Go | Never-claim -> learn | "Working knowledge of at least one of Shell, Terraform, YAML, or Go" |
| Shell / YAML | Missing, learnable | Same language requirement; cheapest one to satisfy |
| AWS EC2 / S3 | Have | "basic exposure to AWS core services (such as EC2, S3, EKS)" |
| EKS / AKS | Missing, learnable | Dual-cloud clusters are the team's substrate |
| Azure basics (VM, Blob, VNet) | Missing, learnable | "dual-cloud infrastructure spanning AWS and Azure" |
| Docker | Have | "containerized infrastructure (Docker, Kubernetes)" |
| CI/CD | Have | "CI/CD pipelines (e.g., Harness or an equivalent)" |
| GitOps / ArgoCD | Missing, learnable | "Some exposure to GitOps workflows (e.g., ArgoCD)" |
| Kafka / event streaming | Have | "asynchronous event streaming (e.g., Kafka)" |
| Metrics/alerts (Grafana) | Have | "observability coverage, including metrics, alerts" |
| OpenTelemetry / distributed tracing | Missing, learnable | "basic distributed tracing" and desired "OpenTelemetry" |
| Canary / blue-green deploys | Missing, learnable | "Curiosity about advanced deployment strategies" |
| OPA/Gatekeeper | Missing, learnable (optional) | "Interest in policy-as-code tools" |
| AI-assisted dev tools (Claude Code) | Missing, learnable | "Practical experience with, or strong desire to learn, AI-assisted development tools" |
| Operating 12B-email-scale systems | Missing, structural | "process more than 12 billion emails during peak events" |
| 1-2+ yrs professional SWE experience | Structural (borderline) | Required qualification; answer with internships/projects honestly |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Kubernetes core objects** (deployments, pods, services, kubectl basics). Resource: the official Kubernetes Basics tutorial (kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/kubernetes-basics). Self-check: in 30 min, from memory, explain what happens when a pod dies under a Deployment and sketch the YAML for one Deployment + one Service.
2. **Shell + YAML fluency** (she must satisfy "at least one of Shell, Terraform, YAML, or Go" with a non-never-claim answer first). Resource: linuxcommand.org "Learning the Shell" + YAML spec 1.2 cheat sheet. Self-check: write a 20-line bash script that parses a YAML file with yq and prints pod names; no notes allowed.
3. **Terraform mental model** (plan/apply, state, HCL blocks) — learn, never claim. Resource: HashiCorp's "Get Started - AWS" tutorial (developer.hashicorp.com). Self-check: explain in 5 minutes what `terraform plan` reads and writes, and why state files shouldn't be committed.
4. **GitOps vocabulary** (ArgoCD: desired state, sync, drift) reacting to "Some exposure to GitOps workflows". Resource: ArgoCD docs "Getting Started" (argo-cd.readthedocs.io). Self-check: whiteboard how a Git commit becomes a running pod via ArgoCD, naming each component.
5. **Observability words** (metrics vs logs vs traces; she has Grafana, add tracing). Resource: OpenTelemetry "Concepts" docs (opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts). Self-check: explain the three signal types and when a trace beats a metric, in under 10 minutes aloud.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **EKS hands-on**: deploy a small containerized API (she knows Docker, Flask) to a free-tier EKS or local kind cluster. Artefact: a repo with Dockerfile, k8s manifests, and a README showing `kubectl get pods` output and a rolling update. Label it "learning project, not production experience."
2. **Terraform + AWS module**: write one Terraform module that provisions an S3 bucket and an EC2 instance (both registered skills, so the cloud side is honest) with remote state. Artefact: the repo plus a written walkthrough of a plan/apply/destroy cycle.
3. **CI/CD + GitOps mini-pipeline**: extend item 1 with a CI workflow (GitHub Actions — CI/CD is registered) that builds, tests, and pushes the image, plus a paragraph comparing push-based CI to ArgoCD pull-based GitOps. Artefact: the working workflow file and the comparison note.
4. **Distributed tracing demo**: instrument her existing Flask API with the OpenTelemetry Python SDK, export to Jaeger locally. Artefact: a notebook or README with screenshots of one trace spanning two services, explaining spans and context propagation.
5. **Go fundamentals** (never-claim -> learn; the team's likely code language). Resource: go.dev/tour. Artefact: a tiny CLI (e.g., a kubectl-style pod-lister against the kind cluster API) in ~150 lines, with tests.

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

She has no Kubernetes/Terraform/self-built-CI-CD project; all existing projects are ML/embedded. **"Mini platform deploy" (not built yet).** Goal: a two-service app (Flask API + worker consuming from a Kafka topic — both registered skills) deployed to a kind cluster. Data: synthetic JSON events (simulated email-send events, nodding to Twilio's domain). Stack: Docker, kind, Terraform for an S3/EC2 sidecar resource, GitHub Actions CI, optional ArgoCD. Evaluation: rolling update with zero failed health checks; one Grafana dashboard; one Jaeger trace. Deliverable: public repo, architecture diagram, 1-page writeup. Hours: ~25-35 over weeks 3-5.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- "I haven't operated systems at billions-of-messages scale. What I bring is strong data-streaming fundamentals from Kafka and Spark projects, and I'm actively building hands-on Kubernetes skills — I'd expect to learn your scale practices from the senior engineers, exactly as this L2 role describes."
- "My professional experience is on the earlier side of the 1-2 year band, so I compensate with depth in fundamentals and a fast learning loop — including the AI-assisted tooling your team uses."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after each skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before, and Kubernetes, Terraform, and Go stay off it until that bar is met.

plan.summary: This OpenAI Scaling-team role centers on porting LLM training/inference workloads to new hardware, building benchmark and stress-test harnesses, and deep NCCL/RDMA performance work; she already has PyTorch, Python, C++, Docker, CI/CD and test automation, but must learn distributed-training internals, GPU profiling and collective-communication basics before interviews. The 5+ years of ML-systems/HPC production experience and hands-on early-hardware lab work are structural gaps that need honest framing, not study.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| PyTorch, Python | Have | "Strong hands-on experience with PyTorch and modern LLM training/inference stacks" |
| C++, Linux, Git | Have | "comfort reading/writing performance-critical code (C++/CUDA/HIP is a plus)" |
| Docker, CI/CD, test automation, Grafana | Have | "repeatable test harnesses that run in CI", "telemetry hooks" |
| Distributed training (data/model/pipeline parallel, collectives) | Learnable | "Large-scale distributed training concepts (data/model/pipeline parallel, collective comms)" |
| NCCL/RCCL concepts + tuning | Learnable (conceptual) | "Collective performance and tuning (across NCCL/RCCL and internal libraries)" |
| GPU profiling: Nsight, perf, flamegraphs, PyTorch profiler | Learnable | "Strong profiling/debugging skills ... ability to reason from traces/counters" |
| CUDA basics | Learnable (reading level) | "C++/CUDA/HIP is a plus"; kernel-level bottleneck analysis |
| RDMA / RoCE / NVLink concepts | Learnable (conceptual) | "Familiarity with RDMA networking and transport tuning" |
| Benchmark/stress-harness design | Learnable | "workload-shaped benchmarks and stress/fault tests that correlate to production behavior" |
| Kubernetes | Never-claim (learn basics only) | "running and validating workloads in Kubernetes" — never say she has it |
| 5+ yrs ML systems / HPC production | Structural | "5+ years in ... ML systems, performance engineering, distributed systems, or HPC" |
| Early-hardware lab bring-up (new NICs/GPUs/racks) | Structural | "Hands-on lab experience with early hardware" |
| BS in CS/EE | Have (education) | Degree held; not a gap |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **Distributed training vocabulary**: data vs tensor vs pipeline parallelism, AllReduce/AllGather, gradient bucketing. Resource: PyTorch DDP tutorial (pytorch.org/tutorials). Self-check: explain in 5 minutes why AllReduce bandwidth, not FLOPs, bounds large-model scaling.
2. **NCCL fundamentals**: what collectives are, ring vs tree algorithms, what NCCL_DEBUG shows. Resource: NCCL documentation (docs.nvidia.com). Self-check: sketch how ring AllReduce moves data across 8 GPUs and name one topology factor that changes it.
3. **GPU profiling literacy**: Nsight Systems timeline vs Nsight Compute kernel metrics, what a flamegraph shows. Resource: PyTorch Profiler tutorial + Nsight Systems user guide. Self-check: profile a toy PyTorch training loop and identify the top kernel and one CPU-GPU sync stall.
4. **RDMA at concept level**: verbs, queue pairs, RoCE vs InfiniBand, why RDMA matters for collectives. Resource: "RDMA Aware Networks" intro posts + NVIDIA RoCE docs. Self-check: explain to a friend why TCP is too slow for NCCL and what congestion does to AllReduce.
5. **Honest self-positioning script**: one sentence per must-have stating what she has done vs only studied. Self-check: say each aloud without overstating.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **Multi-GPU training run**: DDP and FSDP on 2+ GPUs (rented cloud instance OK), measure scaling efficiency. Artefact: small repo with training script + README table of throughput vs GPU count.
2. **NCCL micro-benchmarks**: run NVIDIA nccl-tests (all_reduce_perf), vary message size and transport. Artefact: notebook plotting bandwidth curves with commentary on where topology shows up.
3. **Profiling deep-dive**: take an open-source LLM training step, capture Nsight Systems trace, find one comm/compute overlap opportunity. Artefact: written walkthrough with annotated timeline screenshots.
4. **Workload-shaped benchmark design**: study how MLPerf Training and nvbandwidth structure tests; write a design doc for a stress test that exercises compute + memory + network together, mirroring the JD's "capture real E2E behavior". Artefact: the design doc in the repo.
5. **Regression-detecting harness in CI**: extend item 1 so benchmark results run in CI and flag regressions (she has CI/CD and test automation — combine them). Artefact: repo with workflow file, pass/fail thresholds and a sample regression caught on purpose.

## Build-now project (not built yet)

JD needs a self-built benchmark/CI harness; her projects have none. Spec: Goal — repeatable GPU benchmark + regression harness for a small PyTorch training workload. Data — synthetic tokens + a public tiny model (e.g., GPT-2-small config). Stack — PyTorch DDP, NCCL, Docker, GitHub Actions (no Kubernetes: never-claim). Evaluation — tokens/sec, AllReduce bandwidth, memory bandwidth; fail on >3% regression vs baseline. Deliverable — public repo: harness code, CI workflow, results notebook, one-page writeup of a found bottleneck. Hours — ~40 over weeks 2-5. This is also Tier 2 items 1+5 merged; label it "not built yet".

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

**5+ years ML systems/HPC:** "My production depth is in data and CV pipelines plus embedded/FPGA work, not five years of ML systems — but that hardware-plus-software background is exactly why porting workloads and reading traces across the stack is how I already think."

**Early-hardware lab work:** "I haven't brought up unreleased racks, but I've debugged against bare hardware — FPGA boards, microcontrollers, AXI interfaces — where the datasheet is wrong and you bisect with counters. I know how to write a minimal repro and a bug report a vendor can act on."

**Kubernetes (never-claim):** "I haven't run production Kubernetes; I know the concepts and have containerized workloads with Docker — I'd ramp on your K8s integration fast, but I won't pretend it's deep today."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after a skill is learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.

plan.summary: Western Digital's early-career Software Engineer posting is a pooled requisition spanning five tracks (system tools, applications, data analytics, firmware, systems integration), and her registered skills already cover nearly every named technical requirement — Python, C, C++, Java, SQL, Git, Linux, pipelines, embedded, and dashboards tooling. The plan focuses on the two real gaps (business-facing dashboards and stakeholder translation), WD's storage/semiconductor domain vocabulary, and honest framing of her early-career experience level; no structural gap blocks this role.
plan.report:
## Demand map

| Skill (JD wording) | Bucket | Why the JD wants it |
|---|---|---|
| Python, C, C++, Java, SQL | Have | "one or more programming languages such as C, C++, Python, Java... SQL" |
| Git, Linux, IDEs | Have | "common software development tools (such as Git, Linux, or IDEs)" |
| Data structures, algorithms, debugging, OS concepts | Have | "software development fundamentals, debugging, data structures, algorithms, operating systems" |
| Data pipelines, ETL, automation | Have (Spark, Kafka, Airflow, Flink, AWS Glue) | "Design and develop data pipelines... automation tools for collecting, processing, and analyzing data" |
| Embedded/firmware (C, FreeRTOS, SPI/I2C/UART) | Have | "Write software using C, C++... low-level programming languages" |
| Dashboards, reports, visualizations | Missing, learnable (she has Streamlit + Grafana as base; Tableau/Power BI/Looker are never-claim) | "Create dashboards, reports, and visualizations that support decision-making" |
| Stakeholder translation | Missing, learnable | "Partner with stakeholders to understand business needs and translate them into technical solutions" |
| Storage / semiconductor domain knowledge | Missing, learnable | "Interest in storage technologies, semiconductors... emerging technologies" |
| Data warehouse / dimensional modeling | Missing, learnable (Delta Lake/Databricks base) | "data pipelines, databases, and data warehouses" |
| Compilers / networking tools / "operating systems" internals | Missing, learnable (fundamentals only) | "Build or enhance operating systems, compilers, networking tools" |
| 0–2+ years professional experience | Structural — but the JD targets exactly this band | "aligned with candidates who have approximately 0–2+ years" |
| Degree requirement | Have (BE + MS; a held degree is never a gap) | "Bachelor's or Master's degree in CS... or a related technical field" |
| Go, Tableau, Power BI | Never-claim (Go appears in JD's language list; BI tools implied by "dashboards") — may be learned, never claimed | JD language list; visualization expectations |

## Tier 1 - before the screening call (week 1-2)

1. **WD domain vocabulary: NAND flash and SSDs.** Learn: how flash pages/blocks work, why writes erase-before-write, what an FTL (flash translation layer) does, HDD vs SSD product lines. Resource: WD's own "What is NAND flash" explainers and the SNIA education library (free). Self-check (30 min): explain out loud, unaided, why an SSD slows down as it fills, in 3 minutes.
2. **Dashboard thinking (never-claim tools stay out of mouth).** Learn: what a good operational dashboard contains — KPI choice, refresh cadence, drill-down. Resource: free chapters/articles at storytellingwithdata.com. Self-check: sketch on paper a 4-panel dashboard for monitoring a data pipeline and justify each panel.
3. **Stakeholder translation script.** Learn: the "business need → metric → technical spec" framing for her Medical IoT and expense-tracker projects. Resource: free Google Data Analytics capstone readings on stakeholder questions (Coursera audit). Self-check: write three STAR stories ending in a measurable outcome.
4. **OS internals refresh (system-tools track).** Learn: processes vs threads, virtual memory, syscall path — she has Multithreading, this is depth for questions. Resource: OSTEP (free, ostep.org), chapters on concurrency and memory. Self-check: answer "what happens on a context switch?" in writing, no notes.
5. **Data warehouse basics.** Learn: star schema, fact vs dimension, slowly changing dimensions — she has Delta Lake, this is modeling vocabulary. Resource: Kimball Group's free dimensional modeling design tips. Self-check: model "expense tracker" as one fact table + three dimensions on paper.

## Tier 2 - before the technical round (week 2-5)

1. **SSD write-path walkthrough.** Deep-dive FTL, garbage collection, wear leveling. Artefact: a two-page written walkthrough with a diagram, "What happens when you write 4 KB to an SSD," publishable as a repo README.
2. **C++ systems debugging at depth.** JD: "Troubleshoot, debug, and optimize software performance." Practice gdb, valgrind, perf on deliberately buggy C/C++. Artefact: small repo with a race-condition bug, its perf trace, and the fix, documented.
3. **End-to-end pipeline with a dashboard.** Extend her existing stack (Kafka/Spark → Delta Lake) with a Streamlit or Grafana front end — closes the "dashboards" gap using tools she may claim. Artefact: public repo, sample dataset, screenshot of a live dashboard with 4 KPIs.
4. **Dimensional warehouse mini-build.** Implement the Tier-1 star schema in SQL on Databricks Community Edition (free). Artefact: notebook showing schema, three analytical queries, and a one-paragraph design rationale.
5. **Mock screen rehearsal.** Record herself answering "Tell me about yourself," "Why Western Digital / why storage," and one project deep-dive. Artefact: one 5-minute recording reviewed against a checklist (JD keywords used, honest skill levels stated).

## Build-now project (only if the JD needs a project type she has none of)

Not required. The JD asks for pipelines, applications, embedded systems, and tools — her project list already covers IoT analytics streaming, an LLM application, FPGA/embedded work, and full-stack apps. The Tier-2 pipeline-plus-dashboard extension fills the only thin spot (business-facing visualization) without a new build.

## Honest answers for the structural gaps

- **0–2+ years experience:** "I'm at the very start of the band this role targets — my experience is graduate research and a dozen shipped projects, not production systems at a company yet. That's exactly why an early-career program with structured onboarding appeals to me."
- **No storage-industry background:** "I haven't worked in storage before, but my embedded and FPGA work taught me to think at the hardware-software boundary, and I've spent the last few weeks learning how NAND and SSD firmware actually work — happy to walk you through what I've learned."
- **Dashboards:** "My dashboarding so far is in Streamlit and Grafana rather than enterprise BI tools; the design thinking transfers and I'd ramp on your stack quickly."

## When this may go on the resume

Only after the skill is genuinely learned AND written into data/context/, then re-registered — never before.
